title: Access Sensor Data
text: All data collected by OPDI sensors flows into the OpenSky Network and is accessible through their data interfaces. This page explains how to access the ADS-B data captured by the OPDI sensor fleet and the broader OpenSky Network.

title: Access Sensor Data
text:
OpenSky Network API
The OpenSky Network provides a REST API for real-time and historical ADS-B data. With an OpenSky account, you can query:

Live state vectors — current position, altitude, velocity, and identification of aircraft
Flight tracks — waypoint-based trajectories for individual flights
Arrival and departure data — flights arriving at or departing from specific airports

The API is documented at openskynetwork.github.io/opensky-api.






Registered users with an active feeder receive enhanced API access with higher rate limits and longer historical data access.

OpenSky Historical Database
For research purposes, the OpenSky Network maintains a historical database of ADS-B state vectors with global coverage. Access is available to researchers and academic institutions through an application process.

text:
Using Sensor Data in the OPDI
The OPDI processes raw ADS-B data from the OpenSky Network (including data from OPDI sensors) into structured flight performance datasets: flight lists, flight events, and measurements. These processed datasets are described on the OPDI Data pages.
If you are interested in the raw ADS-B data from specific OPDI sensor locations, you can query the OpenSky Network API filtering by the sensor’s serial number. Contact us at pru-support@eurocontrol.int for sensor identifiers.

title: Data
text:
What is published
OPDI starts from the position reports that aircraft broadcast by radio, received by the OpenSky Network, a network of ground receivers run by volunteers, universities and other organisations. OPDI groups the reports of one aircraft into flights and describes each flight in two ways.

The flight list has one row per flight: the aircraft, call sign, departure and destination airports, first and last time seen, and main times, such as take-off and landing, and the runways used.
The flight events have one row per event. An event is a moment in a flight with a time and a position, for example the take-off, the top of climb, the crossing of a flight level or the entry into a holding pattern. Each row also carries the measurements taken at that event, for example the distance flown since the start of the flight, and the columns of its flight, so one row stands alone.

Columns are listed on the Data dictionary; how each is computed is explained in Algorithms.

The files are in Parquet, a format that stores data by column and that most tools read: Python (pandas, pyarrow, polars), R (arrow), DuckDB, Spark and Trino. A program that reads only some columns or rows reads only part of the file.
Two small files help to find data (columns on the Data dictionary):

A flight index per month, index/flight_index_YYYYMM.parquet: one row per flight of the month and the name of the daily file that holds it.
A catalogue, catalogue.parquet: one row per published day, with the number of flights and events, the time of the first and last event, the file sizes and the versions of the methods used.

title: Data
section: Which day a flight belongs to
text:
Which day a flight belongs to
A flight belongs to the day on which it was first seen, in UTC: the column dof (date of flight). The files of a day hold the flights first seen that day and all their events, also those after midnight: a flight that takes off at 23:30 UTC and lands at 02:00 UTC the next day is in the files of the day it took off, with its landing.
A few events belong to a track with no row in the flight list (3,338 of 6,691,769 events, or 0.05%, on 14 June 2026). The flight list holds only tracks for which a departure or a destination airport could be named (see Departure and destination airports); these tracks had neither. Their events are published in the file of the day their track started, with empty flight columns.

title: Access
text:
Trino
Trino is a database engine that runs SQL directly on files in the cloud.

Getting access
The tables are on the OpenSky Network’s Trino instance, which also holds its own historical database. Researchers and institutions get access on request: see its page on access to its historical database.


Catalog and schema
A table is named catalog.schema.table. Select the catalog and schema once per session:
USE minio.opdi;
The examples use short table names. The catalog and schema names shown here are placeholders until the tables are announced.


Tables and views

Kind

A view is a stored query that looks like a table. The three views have the layout of release v0.0.2, for code written for it (old and new names). Two things differ:

Identifiers are text, not the 64-bit integers of v0.0.2, so rows cannot be joined to v0.0.2 files by identifier.
version holds the version of each method, not “v0.0.2”.

In measurements, every event has a row for the distance flown and one for the time passed, even when empty, as in v0.0.2. Other types (holding and point merge) have a row only when they have a value.
Filter on dof (the date of flight) whenever you can. Each daily file holds one date, so Trino skips the files of other days. Take the flight_id in the examples as a format only; use a real one from the flight list.


Example: flights between two airports on a day
Flights first seen on 14 June 2026 from London Heathrow (ICAO code EGLL) to Paris Charles de Gaulle (LFPG):
SELECT flight_id, flt_id, typecode, first_seen, atot, aldt, last_seen
FROM flight_list
WHERE dof = DATE '2026-06-14'
  AND adep = 'EGLL'
  AND ades = 'LFPG'
ORDER BY atot;
atot and aldt (take-off and landing times) are empty when the take-off or landing was not detected.


Example: all events of one flight in time order
SELECT event_time, type, altitude_ft, distance_flown_nm, time_passed_s, info
FROM flight_events
WHERE dof = DATE '2026-06-14'
  AND flight_id = '3f9a0c1d2b4e5f60_1781412334'
ORDER BY event_time;
info holds extra details as JSON text; its fields, by event type, are in the Data dictionary.


Example: holding time per destination airport on a day
A holding pattern is a loop that an aircraft flies while it waits for permission to continue, most often before landing. It is published as a holding-start and a holding-end event; its duration in seconds is holding_duration_s on holding-end.
SELECT ades,
       count(*)                       AS holdings,
       count(DISTINCT flight_id)      AS flights,
       sum(holding_duration_s) / 60.0 AS holding_minutes
FROM flight_events
WHERE dof = DATE '2026-06-14'
  AND type = 'holding-end'
GROUP BY ades
ORDER BY holding_minutes DESC;
Each holding pattern is counted under the flight’s destination (ades), wherever flown; unknown destinations fall under an empty ades.


Example: time and distance between FIR crossings
A flight information region (FIR) is an area of airspace in which one service provider gives flight information. OPDI publishes a xing-fir event each time a flight passes from one region to another. No column holds the time spent in a region, but two consecutive crossings of one flight give it, when the region entered at the first (fir_to in info) is the region left at the second (fir_from): the differences of time_passed_s and distance_flown_nm are the time and distance flown in it.
WITH crossings AS (
    SELECT flight_id,
           json_extract_scalar(info, '$.fir_to') AS fir,
           time_passed_s,
           distance_flown_nm,
           lead(json_extract_scalar(info, '$.fir_from'))
               OVER (PARTITION BY flight_id ORDER BY event_time) AS next_fir_from,
           lead(time_passed_s)
               OVER (PARTITION BY flight_id ORDER BY event_time) AS next_time_s,
           lead(distance_flown_nm)
               OVER (PARTITION BY flight_id ORDER BY event_time) AS next_distance_nm
    FROM flight_events
    WHERE dof = DATE '2026-06-14'
      AND type = 'xing-fir'
)
SELECT fir,
       count(*)                                  AS visits,
       sum(next_time_s - time_passed_s) / 60.0   AS minutes,
       sum(next_distance_nm - distance_flown_nm) AS distance_nm
FROM crossings
WHERE next_fir_from = fir
GROUP BY fir
ORDER BY minutes DESC;
What this does not count:

the region a flight is in before its first crossing and after its last one, because no event marks where it enters or leaves there;
a visit cut by a reception gap, when the next crossing seen does not leave the region the previous one entered.

The result is a lower bound. See FIR crossings for the limits of the crossings themselves.


Example: the measurements in the shape of release v0.0.2
SELECT e.type AS event_type, m.type, m.value, m.version
FROM measurements AS m
JOIN events AS e ON e.id = m.event_id
WHERE e.flight_id = '3f9a0c1d2b4e5f60_1781412334'
ORDER BY e.event_time;

title: Access
text:
Files

Where the files are
The files of release v2.0.0 are in one published folder, at the public download address above or in the file browser.
<published folder>/
    flight_list/flight_list_YYYYMMDD.parquet      one file per day
    flight_events/flight_events_YYYYMMDD.parquet  one file per day
    index/flight_index_YYYYMM.parquet             one file per month
    catalogue.parquet                             one row per published day
A worldwide day is about 7 MB of flight list and about 410 MB of flight events. To find a known flight, read the month’s flight index first: its column file names the flight list file, and the events file of the same day holds its events.


Python
The OPDI package has a small reader, opdi.published, that needs Python 3.10 or later, pandas, pyarrow and (for the views) DuckDB. opdi[reader] also installs PySpark, but the reader does not start Spark. Install it from the OPDI repository:
pip install "opdi[reader] @ git+https://github.com/euctrl-pru/opdi"
The base address is a web address, an S3 address (a cloud-storage folder reached with Amazon’s S3 protocol, written s3://bucket/folder) or a local folder that holds flight_list/ and flight_events/. Give it with base=, or set OPDI_PUBLISHED_URL once.
import json
from datetime import date

from opdi import published

day = date(2026, 6, 14)
base = "/data/opdi"  # the folder that holds flight_list/ and flight_events/

# 1. Flights from London Heathrow (EGLL) to Paris Charles de Gaulle (LFPG)
flights = published.read_flight_list(day, base=base)
pairs = flights[(flights["adep"] == "EGLL") & (flights["ades"] == "LFPG")]
print(pairs[["flight_id", "flt_id", "typecode", "atot", "aldt"]].sort_values("atot"))

# 2. All events of one flight, in time order
events = published.read_flight_events(day, base=base)
one = events[events["flight_id"] == "3f9a0c1d2b4e5f60_1781412334"]
print(one.sort_values("event_time")[
    ["event_time", "type", "altitude_ft", "distance_flown_nm", "time_passed_s", "info"]
])

# 3. Holding time per destination airport
holds = published.read_flight_events(day, base=base, types=["holding-end"])
per_airport = (
    holds.groupby("ades")
    .agg(holdings=("event_id", "size"), flights=("flight_id", "nunique"),
         minutes=("holding_duration_s", "sum"))
    .assign(minutes=lambda t: t["minutes"] / 60)
    .sort_values("minutes", ascending=False)
)
print(per_airport)

# 4. Time and distance between two FIR crossings, per region entered
fir = published.read_flight_events(day, base=base, types=["xing-fir"])
fir = fir.sort_values(["flight_id", "event_time"])
fir["fir_from"] = fir["info"].map(lambda s: json.loads(s)["fir_from"])
fir["fir_to"] = fir["info"].map(lambda s: json.loads(s)["fir_to"])
following = fir.groupby("flight_id")[["fir_from", "time_passed_s", "distance_flown_nm"]].shift(-1)
spans = fir.assign(
    minutes=(following["time_passed_s"] - fir["time_passed_s"]) / 60,
    distance_nm=following["distance_flown_nm"] - fir["distance_flown_nm"],
)[following["fir_from"] == fir["fir_to"]]
print(spans.groupby("fir_to")[["minutes", "distance_nm"]].sum())
Both readers also take an end date (read_flight_events(date(2026, 6, 1), date(2026, 6, 7), base=base) reads a week) and a list of columns (columns=[...]), which is much faster; a day of events has several million rows (see Tips). The v0.0.2 shapes are one call away:
old_events = published.as_events(events)              # id, flight_id, type, ..., altitude, info
old_measurements = published.as_measurements(events)  # id, event_id, type, value, version
old_flights = published.as_flight_list_v0(flights)    # id, icao24, flt_id, dof, adep, ...


R
With arrow and dplyr, on downloaded files:
library(arrow)
library(dplyr)

# The folder that holds flight_list/ and flight_events/
base <- "/data/opdi"

# 1. Flights from London Heathrow (EGLL) to Paris Charles de Gaulle (LFPG)
flights <- read_parquet(file.path(base, "flight_list", "flight_list_20260614.parquet"))
flights |>
  filter(adep == "EGLL", ades == "LFPG") |>
  select(flight_id, flt_id, typecode, atot, aldt) |>
  arrange(atot)

# All days of flight events as one dataset; filters are applied while reading
events <- open_dataset(file.path(base, "flight_events"))

# 2. All events of one flight, in time order
events |>
  filter(dof == as.Date("2026-06-14"), flight_id == "3f9a0c1d2b4e5f60_1781412334") |>
  select(event_time, type, altitude_ft, distance_flown_nm, time_passed_s, info) |>
  arrange(event_time) |>
  collect()

# 3. Holding time per destination airport
events |>
  filter(dof == as.Date("2026-06-14"), type == "holding-end") |>
  group_by(ades) |>
  summarise(holdings = n(), minutes = sum(holding_duration_s, na.rm = TRUE) / 60) |>
  arrange(desc(minutes)) |>
  collect()

# 4. Time and distance between two FIR crossings, per region entered
fir <- events |>
  filter(dof == as.Date("2026-06-14"), type == "xing-fir") |>
  select(flight_id, event_time, info, time_passed_s, distance_flown_nm) |>
  collect()
details <- lapply(fir$info, jsonlite::fromJSON)
fir$fir_from <- vapply(details, function(x) x$fir_from, character(1))
fir$fir_to <- vapply(details, function(x) x$fir_to, character(1))
fir |>
  arrange(flight_id, event_time) |>
  group_by(flight_id) |>
  mutate(next_from = lead(fir_from),
         next_time_s = lead(time_passed_s),
         next_distance_nm = lead(distance_flown_nm)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(next_from == fir_to) |>
  group_by(fir = fir_to) |>
  summarise(visits = n(),
            minutes = sum(next_time_s - time_passed_s) / 60,
            distance_nm = sum(next_distance_nm - distance_flown_nm)) |>
  arrange(desc(minutes))


DuckDB
DuckDB is a database that runs inside a program or on the command line and reads Parquet files directly, also over https:// and s3://. The SQL is as for Trino, except that the table is a file and the JSON function is json_extract_string:
-- 1. Flights from London Heathrow to Paris Charles de Gaulle
SELECT flight_id, flt_id, typecode, atot, aldt
FROM read_parquet('/data/opdi/flight_list/flight_list_20260614.parquet')
WHERE adep = 'EGLL' AND ades = 'LFPG'
ORDER BY atot;

-- Crossings into each FIR, over every downloaded day
SELECT json_extract_string(info, '$.fir_to') AS fir, count(*) AS crossings
FROM read_parquet('/data/opdi/flight_events/flight_events_*.parquet')
WHERE type = 'xing-fir'
GROUP BY fir
ORDER BY crossings DESC;
From Python, the reader creates DuckDB views over the files, named like the tables and views in Trino, so a query written for one runs on the other:
import duckdb
from datetime import date
from opdi import published

con = duckdb.connect()
con.execute(published.duckdb_views(base="/data/opdi", start=date(2026, 6, 14)))
con.sql("SELECT type, count(*) AS n FROM flight_events GROUP BY type ORDER BY n DESC")
The views are flight_list, flight_events, flight_index (when the folder holds index/), events, measurements and flight_list_v0, as in Trino.
duckdb_views also takes an end date (end=). Without start, it reads every file in a local or S3 folder.

title: Access
text:
Tips

An empty value (NULL) means “not detected” or “not known”, never zero. Count with movement_dep and movement_arr, which say whether a flight list row counts as a departure or an arrival (see Take-off and landing).
Times are in UTC. Altitudes are in feet, distances in nautical miles (NM, 1 NM = 1,852 m) and durations in seconds, as the column names say.
The flight list is sorted by departure airport and first-seen time, and the flight events by flight and time. A filter on these columns reads the least data.
Filter or select first: to read info, filter on type so that only those rows are parsed, and read only the columns and event types you need.

title: PRC Data Challenges
text:
About
The PRC Data Challenges invite data scientists, researchers, and aviation enthusiasts to tackle real-world aviation performance questions using open data. Organised by the Performance Review Commission (PRC) of EUROCONTROL in collaboration with the OpenSky Network, each challenge defines a specific prediction or estimation task, provides curated open datasets, and evaluates submissions on a public leaderboard.
A core objective of the PRC Data Challenges is to foster transparency and reproducibility in aviation analytics. All participating teams are required to publish their code in open Git repositories, making their methodologies fully inspectable and reproducible. This approach aligns with the PRC’s broader mission to democratise access to performance data and analytical methods, enabling independent validation and building a shared body of open, peer-reviewed techniques for the aviation community.
Each edition ranks the submissions by their root mean square error (RMSE) on a test set of flights whose true values the participants do not see. The RMSE is the square root of the average squared difference between the predicted and the true values; it is in the unit of the quantity predicted, and lower is better. The top three teams share a prize of 5,000 EUR.
For more information, visit the PRC Data Challenge programme page.

title: Data quality: availability and accuracy
text:
How often does each OPDI item exist, and when it does, how close is it to an independent record? The figures come from three days processed worldwide with the current methods.

Pages in this section

title: Data quality: availability and accuracy
text:
Two measures: availability and accuracy
They are kept apart and never merged into one figure: an item can be available and wrong, or rare and exact. Found is not the same as correct.
Availability is how often an item exists, measured in two ways.

Among OPDI’s own flights. Of the flights in OPDI’s flight list that could carry the item, the share that do. A departure item (take-off time, off-block time, line-up, …) counts among the flights with a departure airport, an arrival item among those with a destination airport, the other items among all flights. It needs no reference, so it is given for every item and every airport in the world.
Against a reference. Of the movements in an independent record, the share for which OPDI has the item. It also counts flights OPDI did not receive at all, so it is the better measure of what a study will miss where a reference exists.

Accuracy is how close the item is to the reference when both exist. For a time, it is the share of OPDI’s times within 60 s of the recorded time, with the median and the 90th percentile of the difference. For an airport, runway, stand or aircraft type, it is the share equal to the record. For the distance flown, it is the share within 10 % of the route length that Network Manager records.

title: Data quality: availability and accuracy
text:
In brief

Take-off and landing times are the most reliable times. At the European airports that send airport records, 80.8 % of the recorded take-offs and 81.7 % of the recorded landings have an OPDI time, and 93.2 % and 94.5 % of those times are within 60 s of the record.
Block times are limited by reception on the ground. Only 35.0 % of the recorded off-blocks and 33.4 % of the recorded in-blocks have an OPDI time; 40.3 % of the off-block times and 72.0 % of the in-block times are within 60 s.
Departure and destination airports, runways and aircraft type agree with the records in most cases where they exist; the destination airport is missing more often than the departure airport (why).
Distance circle crossings at 40 and 100 NM are close to the records: most of them within a few seconds.
Events in the air with no reference (tops of climb and descent, level segments, flight-level and FIR crossings, holds, point merge) are given with their availability only.

title: Data quality: availability and accuracy
text:
What OPDI is compared with

Airport records. The movement records that airport operators send to EUROCONTROL: off-block, take-off, landing and in-block times, runway, stand, and the times at which the flight crossed the 40 NM and 100 NM circles around the airport. Not every airport sends them (see Which airports). Many round times to the whole minute, so differences under about half a minute cannot be judged; labels use 60 s.
Network Manager records. EUROCONTROL’s records of every flight in or through European airspace: departure and destination airport, aircraft type, route length, and a take-off and landing time. Its take-off time is the off-block time plus a taxi time, so its times are estimates. They are used for times only at European airports that send no airport records.
No reference. For many items nothing exists to compare with (no record gives a top of climb or a holding pattern), and outside Europe there are no airport records at all; Network Manager knows only the flights to and from Europe there. These items get availability among OPDI’s own flights only.

Records are matched to the nearest OPDI flight within 6 hours by aircraft address (the transponder’s 24-bit code), call sign and airport. Records without an address are not matched or counted. A movement whose flight belongs to the previous day (for example a landing just after midnight) counts as not found, so availability against a reference is slightly low at each day’s ends.

What this means for your study

Taxi-out and taxi-in times need a block time and a runway time of the same flight, and off-block times are often late. Restrict a taxi-time study to airports labelled good or fair for off-block (or in-block) and report how many flights remain. Runway times and runway use can be studied at most European airports that send records. Separate the two methods with info.method when comparing airports: they have different errors.
Arrival flows at 40 and 100 NM (for example additional time in the terminal area) can use the circle crossings; they are close to the records.
Outside Europe, a high availability says the item exists, not that it is right.
Events with no reference suit comparisons between airports, days or airlines computed the same way, but no figure says how close they are to the truth.

Level-offs in climb and descent

Based on

title: Line-up and take-off roll
text: line-up is the first report of a departing aircraft on the runway, and take-off-roll the moment it starts to accelerate along it for take-off.

title: Line-up and take-off roll
text: line-up is the first report of a departing aircraft on the runway, and take-off-roll the moment it starts to accelerate along it for take-off.

title: Line-up and take-off roll
text:
What it needs

A departure runway pass with a take-off, as described on Take-off and landing times: the reports of one track on one runway and its approach areas, classified as a departure.
At least one report on the runway itself, between the two thresholds and within half the runway’s width of its centre line.
Evidence that the take-off started on the ground (step 1 below).

title: Line-up and take-off roll
text:
How it is computed

A take-off from the ground. The two events are given only when the take-off started on the ground: the track has a report flagged on the ground, or slower than 50 kt, in the 60 s before the first report of the pass faster than 50 kt; or, when reception starts during the roll, that first fast report is itself flagged on the ground. A touch-and-go, a low approach or a track that is first received in the air keeps its ATOT but gets neither event.
line-up is the first report of the pass that lies on the runway itself (not in the approach area before the threshold). It is a received report; its time is not interpolated.
Ground speed. Reports on the ground rarely carry a speed (almost none do). Where a report has none, its speed is worked out from its position and the position of the previous report, when the two are at most 30 s apart. A report without any speed is skipped; it does not end the run.
take-off-roll is the first report of the first run of reports with a ground speed of at least 50 kt that lasts at least 5 s, with no silence of more than 30 s inside it. Taxiing is about 20 kt and rotation about 140 kt, so 50 kt separates the take-off run from taxiing; the 5 s keeps a fast turn-off from counting.

title: Line-up and take-off roll
text:
Based on

Developed for OPDI, on the runway passes of the runway-pass method.
The A-CDM Implementation Manual has no line-up or take-off roll milestone: its off-block (milestone 15) is followed directly by take-off (16). The codes T06 and T07 in info.milestone are labels in the PRU flight diagram, not the manual’s numbers; see Milestones of a flight.

Time on the runway before take-off: ATOT minus line-up. A long value points to a wait on the runway for a take-off clearance.
Length of the take-off run: distance_flown_nm at ATOT minus that at take-off-roll, for example per aircraft type.
Runway entry points: the positions of line-up show which entries of a runway are used.

Limitations
Both events are missing when reception starts at lift-off. When reception starts during the roll, the events mark the first report received on the runway, which is later than the real moment. See Limitations: runway events.

title: Top of climb and top of descent
text: top-of-climb marks where the climb to cruise ends and top-of-descent where the final descent starts, by the method of EUROCONTROL’s vertical flight efficiency indicators.
crumbs: Top of climb and top of descent

title: Top of climb and top of descent
text: top-of-climb marks where the climb to cruise ends and top-of-descent where the final descent starts, by the method of EUROCONTROL’s vertical flight efficiency indicators.
crumbs: Top of climb and top of descent

title: Top of climb and top of descent
text:
What it needs

The barometric altitude of the track after cleaning (see Cleaning of position reports). Altitudes below −2,000 ft or above 60,000 ft, and altitudes of reports flagged on the ground, are not used: transponders on the ground sometimes send altitudes of 9,800 to 126,000 ft.
The departure and destination airports of the flight list, for the 200 NM circles around them. Without one of them, the start or end of the track is used instead.
The level segments of the track (see Level segments).
crumbs: Top of climb and top of descent

title: Top of climb and top of descent
text:
How it is computed

Analysis area. For each report, compute the great-circle distance to the departure and destination airports. Find the first moment the aircraft is 200 NM or more from the departure airport (D200; the end of the track if it never is) and the last moment it is more than 200 NM from the destination airport (A200; the start of the track if it never is). A step climb further than 200 NM out is cruise, not climb.
First estimate. The top of climb is the first moment the aircraft reaches its highest altitude between the start of the track and D200. The top of descent is the last moment it is at its highest altitude between A200 and the end of the track. info.d200_time and info.d200_altitude_ft keep this estimate.
Exclusion box. The box runs from the estimated top’s altitude down to 90% of it. A level segment inside the box that lasts more than 300 s is cruise. If one starts before the estimated top of climb, the top of climb moves to the start of the first such segment, at its altitude; the top of descent likewise moves to the end of the last such segment after its estimate. info.relocated says whether the top moved.
Position. The top takes the position of the report with a position nearest in time to it, within 60 s; without one it has no position.
Observed or at the edge of reception. info.observed is true on a top of climb when the track has an altitude at least 3,000 ft lower before it, and on a top of descent when it has one at least 3,000 ft lower after it. Otherwise the top sits where reception starts or ends (a track first received in cruise) and info.observed is false.

Each track has at most one top of climb and one top of descent.
crumbs: Top of climb and top of descent

title: Top of climb and top of descent
text:
Based on

Follows the definition of the top of climb and top of descent in the vertical flight efficiency method of the EUROCONTROL Performance Review Unit (Peeters and Guastalla, 2017): the 200 NM points D200 and A200, the first (climb) or last (descent) point of highest altitude, and the exclusion box from the top down to 90% of it, in which a level segment of more than 5 minutes moves the top (the manual’s ToC-CCO and ToD-CDO).
The position rule (step 4) and info.observed (step 5) were added for OPDI.

Descent planning: the distance from top-of-descent to ALDT, from distance_flown_nm.

text:
Limitations
A flight without a real cruise (a short flight, a training flight) gets its highest report as tops, and a track holding several flights gets only one pair. Use info.observed to leave out tops at the edge of reception. See Limitations: vertical profile.

title: Tracks and flight identity
text: A track is the run of position reports of one aircraft that OPDI treats as one flight; each track is one row of the flight list, identified by flight_id.

title: Tracks and flight identity
text: A track is the run of position reports of one aircraft that OPDI treats as one flight; each track is one row of the flight list, identified by flight_id.

title: Tracks and flight identity
text:
What it needs

The state vectors of the OpenSky Network: one row per aircraft and second, built from the ADS-B messages (Automatic Dependent Surveillance–Broadcast) that aircraft send about once a second, with position, altitude, speed, heading and vertical rate.
Two fields of each state vector identify the aircraft: the ICAO 24-bit address (icao24), six hexadecimal characters set in the transponder, which normally stays with one aircraft for years; and the call sign (flt_id), the radio name of the flight, which changes from flight to flight and is sometimes blank or garbled.

title: Tracks and flight identity
text:
How it is computed

Thin. When the state vectors are read, each aircraft’s reports are thinned to one per 5 seconds: in each 5-second window the newest report is kept.
Group by aircraft. All reports with the same ICAO 24-bit address are taken together, in time order. The call sign is not part of the grouping, so a blank call sign does not start a track of its own.
A new call sign starts a new track only when it lasts: blank call signs are skipped, and a new call sign counts only if it stays the same for at least 30 s before the next change. It is compared with the last call sign heard in the previous 30 minutes. A call sign that flickers to a garbled value and back does not split the flight.
A short silence at low altitude starts a new track. If no report arrives for more than 15 minutes and the aircraft is below 5,000 ft when it is heard again, a new track starts: it may have landed and taken off again out of reception.
A long silence starts a new track unless both sides fit one flight. A silence of more than 30 minutes is a gap. The gap stays inside one track only when every check below passes; a check that lacks a value fails.








Check
Setting
Why




Gap not too long
at most 600 minutes
A longer silence leaves room for anything.


En route before the gap
lowest of the 5 nearest altitudes within 5 minutes before the gap at or above 18,000 ft; if lower, climbing faster than 500 ft/min on at least 3 values
Lost at cruise or still climbing out.


En route after the gap
the same at the other side; between 5,000 and 18,000 ft, descending faster than 500 ft/min on at least 3 values
Reappears in cruise or on its descent.


No descent then climb
not both descending faster than 500 ft/min before and climbing faster than 500 ft/min after
That is what a stop inside the gap looks like.


Call sign agrees
the last call sign before (at most 60 minutes old) and the first after (within 10 minutes) are not both present and different
A different call sign is a different flight.


Straight-line speed
between 400 and 750 kt: the great-circle distance between the two sides divided by the time between them
A stop uses up time; faster than 750 kt means two aircraft share one address.


Real address
not 000000, 000001 or ffffff
These placeholder values are used by many aircraft.



The values at each side are read past blank reports, within 5 minutes of the gap, because position and altitude arrive in separate messages. A gap kept inside a track stays empty: no position is invented, and the event detectors work on each piece between gaps.
Name the track. flight_id is the first 16 characters of the SHA-256 hash of the ICAO address, an underscore, and the time of the track’s first report in seconds since 1970-01-01 (Unix time).
Date and call sign. dof is the date of the track’s first report: a track belongs to the day it starts, with all its reports even when it ends the next day. A day’s run reads 11 hours of the previous day, so a gap near midnight is decided in the same way on both days. flt_id is the call sign the track broadcast most often, without the spaces OpenSky pads it with.

title: Processing steps
text:
OPDI is a chain of numbered steps. Each step reads the tables written by the steps before it and writes its own. The chain runs once per day of data. This page describes the steps of release v2.0.0 with their default settings. The pages listed in Algorithms describe each algorithm in detail.
On the OpenSky Network’s cluster, with 12 Spark executors (worker processes of 2 processor cores each), one worldwide day takes about 6,200 s (1.7 hours) from step 01 to step 09; most of it is spent building the tracks (step 02) and the events (step 04). Part of this figure was scaled up from a measurement over part of the day.

Airports and runways from OurAirports, an open database of the world’s airports: position, elevation, type (large, medium, small, heliport), scheduled service, and the ends of each runway.
Aircraft from the OpenSky aircraft database: registration, model, ICAO type code and operator for each ICAO 24-bit address.
Airport detection zones: for each large and medium airport, the H3 cells around it. H3 is a system that divides the Earth into hexagonal cells at several sizes; resolution 7 cells cover about 5 km² each. The zones let step 03 find the airports near a position quickly.
Airport layouts: the runways, runway thresholds, taxiways, aprons, stands, hangars and de-icing pads of each airport from OpenStreetMap, filled with H3 cells of resolution 12 (about 300 m² each).
Runway and approach grid: H3 cells along each runway and its approach, used by the runway events.
Airspace: the flight information regions (FIRs) of the EUROCONTROL Network Manager airspace model, AIRAC cycle 524, filled with H3 cells. An AIRAC cycle is the 28-day period in which a set of aeronautical data, such as airspace boundaries, is in force.
Point merge systems: a table of merge points and their leg distances.

title: Processing steps
text:
01 Read state vectors
Reads the OpenSky Network archive of state vectors: one row per aircraft and second, with position, barometric and geometric altitude, ground speed, heading, vertical rate, call sign and on-ground flag. Writes the state vectors OPDI keeps.
The whole world is read by default. For each aircraft, one state vector is kept per 5-second window: the newest. See Trajectory cleaning.

title: Processing steps
text:
02 Build tracks
Reads the state vectors of step 01. Writes the tracks: the same state vectors with a track identifier.
The state vectors of each aircraft are split into tracks, one per flight, and each track gets its identifier (published as flight_id). See Track identity. The step also adds, for each state vector, its H3 cells at resolutions 7 and 12, and empties altitudes that change faster than 200 ft/s from the previous sample.
A day’s run reads 11 hours before the day and 24 hours after it, and keeps the tracks whose first state vector falls on that day. A flight that crosses midnight therefore belongs, whole, to the day it started.

title: Processing steps
text:
02a Clean tracks
Reads the tracks. Writes the cleaned tracks: the same rows, with duplicate rows removed and repeated, impossible or isolated values emptied. See Trajectory cleaning.

title: Processing steps
text:
03 Flight list
Reads the cleaned tracks, the airport detection zones and the aircraft database. Writes the flight list: one row per track.
Each row gets the departure and destination airports (see Departure and destination airports), the first and last time the flight was seen, and the aircraft data.

title: Processing steps
text:
04 Events and measurements
Reads the cleaned tracks, the flight list and the reference tables. Writes the events, each with its measurements.
All event families run here: take-off and landing, runway and block times, airport surface events, vertical events, distance rings, holding, point merge, FIR crossings, and first and last seen. Each event gets the distance flown and time passed since the track’s first_seen (see Measurements). Events that compare neighbouring samples work separately on each stretch of a track between two reception gaps. Before anything is written, the plausibility checks leave out the events that the track itself contradicts, such as an in-block time while the aircraft is still flying; those events are kept with the reason in a working table (opdi_flight_events_rejected) that is not published. A removed event is not published, its measurements go with it, and it is not used for the milestone columns of the flight list. A check fires only when every fact it needs is known; when one is unknown, the event is kept.

title: Processing steps
text:
04b Milestones into the flight list
Reads the events and the flight list. Writes the flight list again, with more columns.
The main milestones are copied from the events into the flight list, so that one row holds the whole flight: actual take-off and landing times (atot, aldt), off-block and in-block times (aobt, aibt), runways, stands, and the times of crossing circles of 40, 50, 60, 100, 110 and 120 NM around the airports. This step detects nothing new; a column is empty when the event behind it is missing.
It also adds quality columns: track_duration_min, superseded_dep and superseded_arr (a row that is a piece of a movement already counted on another row) and movement_dep and movement_arr (whether the row counts as a departure or an arrival).

title: Processing steps
text:
09 Publish
Reads the flight list and the events. Writes the published files.
For each day:

flight_list/flight_list_YYYYMMDD.parquet: one row per flight that started that day.
flight_events/flight_events_YYYYMMDD.parquet: one row per event of those flights, with the event’s measurements and the columns of its flight. A flight keeps all its events in the file of the day it started, also those after midnight.

Two small files help to find data: a monthly flight index (index/flight_index_YYYYMM.parquet), which says which file holds a flight, and a catalogue (catalogue.parquet) with one row per published day.
The files are Parquet, a column-based file format that most data tools read. Rows are sorted (the flight list by departure airport and first-seen time, the events by flight and time) so that a reader can skip the parts it does not need.
Steps 05 to 08 produce other export formats and monitoring statistics. They are not needed for the published files and are not described here.

title: FIR crossings
text: An xing-fir event marks each moment a flight passes from one flight information region (FIR), or upper information region (UIR), to another.

title: FIR crossings
text: An xing-fir event marks each moment a flight passes from one flight information region (FIR), or upper information region (UIR), to another.

title: FIR crossings
text:
What it needs

The FIR and UIR volumes of the EUROCONTROL Network Manager airspace model, for AIRAC cycle 524 (valid 2024-11-28 to 2024-12-26). An AIRAC cycle is the 28-day period in which aeronautical data such as airspace boundaries take effect. Each volume has a lateral boundary and a lowest and highest flight level.
The cleaned positions and barometric altitudes of the track’s reports.

title: FIR crossings
text:
How it is computed

Grid. Before any flight is processed, every volume is filled with H3 cells: as small as resolution 7 (about 5 km² each) along the boundaries, larger inside.
Lookup. Each report whose position survived cleaning is placed in the volume whose cells contain its position and whose flight-level band contains its altitude. Where two volumes overlap, the one with the narrowest level band wins, then the one with the smallest area.
Short stays. A stay in one volume shorter than 60 s is counted as part of the volume before it, so a flight along a boundary does not cross it at every cell.
Crossing. A crossing is a change of volume between two consecutive stays. A stretch with no volume in between (for example where the altitude was removed by cleaning) does not count as leaving and entering again. The event sits on the first report in the new volume.
A crossing whose two reports imply more than 1,000 kt (a position that jumped) is not given.
info.vertical is true when the two volumes lie one above the other (their flight-level bands do not overlap), as a FIR and the UIR above it: the crossing is then a climb or descent through the boundary level, not a lateral crossing.

Nothing is computed across a reception gap of more than 30 minutes kept inside a track.

title: FIR crossings
text:
Based on

The volumes are those of the EUROCONTROL Network Manager airspace model, as published in the PRU Atlas. The grid is H3.
The lookup and the rules of steps 3 to 6 were developed for OPDI.

Flights and distance per region: the difference of distance_flown_nm between two consecutive crossings of a flight is the distance flown in one region.
Traffic entering a region per hour, for example to compare with capacity.
Lateral crossings only: leave out the crossings with info.vertical true.

The same AIRAC cycle is used for every day, so a boundary changed since then is not followed. See Limitations: FIR crossings.

title: Distance flown
text: distance_flown_nm is the distance the aircraft flew from the start of its track to the event, along its received positions, in nautical miles (1 NM = 1,852 m).

title: Distance flown
text: distance_flown_nm is the distance the aircraft flew from the start of its track to the event, along its received positions, in nautical miles (1 NM = 1,852 m).

title: Distance flown
text:
What it needs
The cleaned positions of the track’s reports (see Cleaning of position reports).

title: Distance flown
text:
How it is computed

Sort the track’s reports by time.
For each report with a position, compute the great-circle distance from the last earlier report with a position (Earth radius 6,371 km; altitude is not taken into account).
Jumps. A step that implies more than 1,000 kt (with 2 NM of tolerance) is not added: the position jumped (a spoofed or shifted position, or two aircraft under one address). A position that jumps away and back is treated as missing. The next step starts from the new position.
Add up the steps from the start of the track. Across a gap, the straight line between its two sides is added: the shortest distance the aircraft could have flown.
At the event. An event on a report with a position takes the sum there. An event between reports, or on a report without a position, gets the distance interpolated in time between the positioned reports before and after it in the same piece of track. Events whose family gives no distance (block times, for example) get the distance interpolated between the events before and after them.
Before the first known position the distance is empty, not 0. No value is written when there is none.

title: Distance flown

Distance between two events of one flight: the difference of their distance_flown_nm, for example from xing-40nm inbound to ALDT.

Counted from the start of the track, not from the departure airport: a track first received in the air starts later. Gaps add a straight line, so the distance is a lower bound. See Limitations: measurements.

title: Take-off and landing times
text: ATOT is the moment the wheels leave the runway and ALDT the moment they touch it, found from the aircraft’s own position reports over the runway, or, where those are missing, from the first reports of the climb or the last reports of the descent.

title: Take-off and landing times
text: ATOT is the moment the wheels leave the runway and ALDT the moment they touch it, found from the aircraft’s own position reports over the runway, or, where those are missing, from the first reports of the climb or the last reports of the descent.

title: Take-off and landing times
text:
What it needs

The cleaned position reports of the track (one every 5 seconds; see Cleaning of position reports).
The departure and destination airports of the flight list, and the other airports close to the start and the end of the track (see Departure and destination airports). Runway events are looked for only at these airports.
The runways of the airport from OurAirports, an open database of airports: the position of each end (threshold), the length and the width. The true bearing of a runway is computed from its two thresholds.
For the first method: reports on the runway or less than 1 NM short of it. For the second: reports in the first or last 1,500 ft of the flight within 5 NM of the airport.

title: Take-off and landing times
text:
How it is computed
Two methods give the time. The first, the runway-pass method (written acdm in info.method), follows the aircraft on the runway. The second, the runway-window method (legacy), reads the initial climb or the final descent. The published time comes from the first method when it finds one, and from the second otherwise.

Height above the ground
Both methods need the height of the aircraft above the runway. Aircraft report a barometric altitude, measured from air pressure against the standard pressure of 1013.25 hPa. On a day of low or high pressure an aircraft standing on the runway reads several hundred feet above or below the airport’s elevation (from −571 to +232 ft on one measured day). OPDI therefore measures height from the aircraft’s own altitude on the ground:

At each airport the track visits, take its reports at the runways that are flagged on the ground by the transponder, or slower than 30 kt and not climbing or descending faster than 300 ft/min. Airliners send no altitude on the ground, so the reports with an altitude within 30 s of these are read too.
Among their altitudes, take the highest that is at most 30 ft above the lowest (altitudes come in steps of 25 ft). This is the track’s ground altitude at that airport. A track that lands, stands and departs again gets one ground altitude per visit (a silence of more than 300 s starts a new visit).
When the track has no such report, or the result is more than 1,000 ft from the airport’s published elevation, the published elevation is used. info.height_reference says which was used (track or elevation).



Runway-pass method (method = acdm)

Runway grid. Each runway of each large and medium airport is covered with H3 cells of resolution 12 (each about 300 m²). H3 is an open grid that divides the Earth into hexagons. The grid holds the runway itself and, at each end, an approach area reaching 1 NM out from the threshold.
Runway pass. The reports of a track whose cell lies in the grid of one runway, in time order, form a runway pass. A silence of more than 300 s starts a new pass.
Direction of the runway. Each runway has two directions (for example 07 and 25). The direction of a pass is the one within 90° of the aircraft’s median direction of travel over the ground (its ground track), taken over the reports faster than 50 kt. One pass per runway is kept. Of passes of the same kind on parallel runways at overlapping times, the one with reports on its own runway and the smallest median distance from its centre line is kept.
Kind of pass. The pass is a departure when the angle between the ground track and the runway is at most 30°, the highest ground speed is above 50 kt, the height is below 15 ft at the start and at least 15 ft at the end, and the pass ends in the air: neither the report that gives the end height nor the last report of the pass is flagged on the ground. A circuit (take-off and landing on one runway a few minutes apart) is still a departure when the pass holds two reports in the air between 100 and 3,000 ft above the ground. The pass is an arrival under the mirror conditions: angle at most 30°, faster than 50 kt, at least 15 ft at the start and below 15 ft at the end. A pass at an angle between 30° and 45° gives no event: naming no movement is better than naming the wrong one.
ATOT is the moment the height rises through 15 ft, and ALDT the moment it falls through 15 ft. The time and position are interpolated in a straight line between the two reports either side. A dead band of 5 ft on each side (the height must pass from below 10 ft to above 20 ft) keeps a short bounce from giving two times. A report without altitude is skipped; a report with an altitude but no position takes the position interpolated between the positioned reports before and after it when both are within 30 s. When the two reports either side of 15 ft are more than 60 s apart, no time is given (info.bracket_s holds that time).



Runway-window method (method = legacy)
This method follows the runway detection of the traffic library and is used at the departure and destination airports of the flight list only.

Keep the reports within 5 NM of the airport, at most 1,500 ft above its published elevation, faster than 30 kt and climbing (for a departure) or descending (for an arrival) faster than 257 ft/min.
At least 4 reports must remain: they are the initial climb or the final descent.
Runway. The candidate runways are those whose direction is within 10° of the median ground track of these reports; the one whose centre line is nearest to their median position wins.
Only reports at most 0.5 NM from that runway’s extended centre line count. For a landing, a report on the ground (flagged, or slower than 50 kt) must follow when the track continues for more than 120 s.
Time. The take-off time is the time of the earliest of these reports, and the landing time the time of the latest. The event takes that report’s position and altitude. info.at_track_edge is true when the report is the first report of the track (take-off) or its last (landing): reception then started in the climb or ended on final approach.
Height check. The time is kept only when its report is at most 1,500 ft above the track’s ground altitude at the airport, on the same visit (see Height above the ground). Step 1 already keeps only reports at most 1,500 ft above the published elevation, so this check removes a time only when the ground altitude reads below the elevation (on a day of high pressure, because the altitude is measured against standard pressure). Where the ground reads at or above the elevation, or no ground altitude is known, it removes nothing.



One take-off and one landing per track and airport

Each track keeps at most one ATOT and one ALDT at each airport (info.apt_icao): the runway-pass time when there is one (the earliest take-off and the latest landing), otherwise the runway-window time. Two readings of one movement are at one airport and give one event; a track that holds several flights keeps the landing at a stop on the way and the landing at its destination.
The plausibility checks remove an ATOT or ALDT more than 1,500 ft above the ground at its airport. When the height comes from the elevation rather than the track, 1,000 ft is added to that limit for the error of barometric altitude.

title: Take-off and landing times
text:
Based on

Runway-window method: a port of the take-off runway detection of the traffic library (TrackBasedRunwayDetection), with its limits: within 5 NM of the airport, below 1,500 ft, faster than 30 kt, climbing faster than 257 ft/min, at least 4 reports and runways within 10°. traffic detects take-offs only; OPDI applies the mirror rule to landings, measures height above the track’s ground altitude and adds the checks of steps 4 and 6.
Runway-pass method: developed for OPDI.
Definitions: ATOT and ALDT are the take-off (milestone 16) and landing (milestone 6) of the A-CDM Implementation Manual. The codes T08 and T17 in info.milestone are labels in the PRU flight diagram, not the manual’s numbers; see Milestones of a flight.
Related work: Schultz, Rosenow and Olive (2022) derive ATOT and ALDT from ADS-B by the change of the “on the ground” flag, a simpler rule than either OPDI method.
Data: runways from OurAirports, runway grid on H3.

title: Take-off and landing times
text:
What is published
Event types ATOT and ALDT in the flight events file, with position, altitude, distance_flown_nm and time_passed_s. Their info holds apt_icao (airport), runway (direction, for example 25R), runway_bearing_deg and method (acdm or legacy). Times of the runway-pass method also carry traversal_class, align_deg, max_gs_kt, milestone, bracket_s and height_reference; times of the runway-window method carry role, bearing_error_deg, n_samples and at_track_edge. Every field is listed in the Data dictionary.
The flight list repeats them: atot and rwy_dep, rwy_dep_bearing_deg from the earliest ATOT at the departure airport; aldt and rwy_arr, rwy_arr_bearing_deg from the latest ALDT at the destination airport (see Milestone columns of the flight list).

title: Take-off and landing times
text:
Use cases

Taxi-out and taxi-in times per airport: ATOT minus AOBT, and AIBT minus ALDT, of the same flight. Both events must exist, which depends on reception on the ground at the airport.
Runway use: count take-offs and landings per runway direction and hour from info.runway, for example to see when an airport changes direction.
Time in the air: ALDT minus ATOT. A track that holds several flights has one of each per airport it visits: pair them by info.apt_icao and time.

title: Take-off and landing times
text:
Limitations
The time is missing when the aircraft was not received near the runway, and runway-window times (legacy) are less precise than runway-pass times (acdm); use info.method to separate them. See Limitations: take-off and landing.

text: The milestone columns put the main events of a flight on its flight-list row, taken from the events of the same track at the row’s own departure and destination airports.

title: Milestone columns of the flight list
text: The milestone columns put the main events of a flight on its flight-list row, taken from the events of the same track at the row’s own departure and destination airports.

title: Milestone columns of the flight list
text:
What it needs

The flight events of the track (see each event’s page).
The departure and destination airports of the row, after the correction by runway events (see Departure and destination airports).

title: Milestone columns of the flight list
text:
How it is computed

Take-off and landing. atot is the earliest ATOT event at the departure airport, and rwy_dep and rwy_dep_bearing_deg the runway and its bearing from the same event. aldt is the latest ALDT at the destination airport, with rwy_arr and rwy_arr_bearing_deg.
Block times. aobt is the latest AOBT at the departure airport that is not after atot; aibt the earliest AIBT at the destination airport that is not before aldt.
Stands. stnd_dep is the stand named by that AOBT, otherwise the stand of the last exit-parking_position at the departure airport before atot. stnd_arr is the stand named by that AIBT, otherwise that of the first entry-parking_position at the destination airport after aldt.
Distance circles. For each radius (40, 50, 60, 100, 110 and 120 NM), c{radius}_dep is the first outbound crossing around the departure airport after atot, and c{radius}_arr the last inbound crossing around the destination airport before aldt.
Where the take-off or landing time is unknown, the time limit of steps 2 to 4 is not applied. An event that names no airport is accepted. On a row with no departure airport, an AOBT read at a named stand is kept, with that stand in stnd_dep: the stand passage is its evidence, and the row has no airport to contradict it. The same holds for an AIBT on a row with no destination airport. A column is empty when no event qualifies.

title: Milestone columns of the flight list
text:
Based on
Developed for OPDI. The events behind each column are described on their own pages: Take-off and landing times, Off-block and in-block times, Airport surface events and Distance circle crossings.

title: Airport surface events
text: An entry-{element} event marks when an aircraft enters an area of an airport, and the matching exit-{element} event when it leaves it, where {element} is the kind of area.

title: Airport surface events
text:
What it needs

The airport layout from OpenStreetMap, the open map of the world, for the large and medium airports: the areas mapped there as taxiways, aprons, stands, threshold markings, hangars and de-icing pads.
Reports of the track with a position on the airport surface, at an airport that the flight list names for the flight (the departure or destination airport, or one of the other close airports listed).

title: Airport surface events
text:
How it is computed

The layout

Each area is read from OpenStreetMap. An area mapped as a line (a taxiway centre line) or a point (a stand) is widened into a surface, with the width given in OpenStreetMap or a default width for its kind (for example 30 m for a taxiway and 25 m for a stand).
Each surface is covered with H3 cells of resolution 12, each about 300 m² (about 20 m across). H3 is an open grid that divides the Earth into hexagons.



Passages

Reports used. A report flagged on the ground by the transponder is always used. A report not flagged on the ground is used only when it is at most 300 ft above the airport and at most 50 kt fast (the speed is the largest of the reported speed and the speeds from its positions to the reports just before and after it, when at most 30 s apart; a report with no known speed is used). Aircraft on approach, climbing out or passing low over the airport are left out.
Match. A report is in an area when its H3 cell is one of the area’s cells.
Passage. The matched reports of one track in one area, in time order, form a passage. A silence of more than 300 s starts a new passage. A passage of a single report, or whose first and last reports fall in the same second, is dropped.
One area per passage. Areas of one kind often overlap (a taxiway drawn as several lines, a stand drawn over a taxi lane). The area is chosen once per passage, so every entry has its exit on the same area: of passages of one kind that start (or end) at the same report, the longest is kept, but of stands the shortest (the stand itself rather than a larger area drawn around it). Where a stand is drawn inside a larger stand area, both passages are published, and the larger one is marked info.encloses_stand.
Parked aircraft. Two consecutive passages of one area are joined when the aircraft moved less than 165 ft (about 50 m) between them and entered no other area in between. A parked aircraft whose position jitters across the edge of an area then gives one passage. Stand passages are not joined: the exit before a silence at the stand is often the off-block.
Events. The first report of a passage gives the entry- event and the last gives the exit- event, each with that report’s position, altitude and measurements.
Marks. info.at_track_start is set on an entry made at the track’s first report with a position, and info.at_track_end on an exit made at its last: reception started or stopped there, the aircraft did not move. info.ground_only is set on the events of a track that never leaves the ground and whose aircraft type is unknown or a vehicle type, in practice an airport vehicle.
The plausibility checks remove an entry or exit made while the aircraft flies (more than 1,500 ft above the airport, faster than 80 kt and no report on the ground within 60 s).

The runway itself has no surface event: its use is described by the runway events.

title: Airport surface events
text:
Based on

The method of mapping an airport’s layout onto the H3 grid comes from HexAeroPy (Goens, EUROCONTROL), the tool that finds the airports, runways, taxiways and stands used by a flight from its positions.
The airport areas come from OpenStreetMap (its aeroway features); the grid is H3.
The passage rules (steps 3 to 9) were developed for OPDI.
Related published work: Olive, Waltert and Schultz (2025) also match ADS-B positions on the ground to OpenStreetMap taxiways, to measure taxi times and congestion.

title: Where Next
section: Where does OPDI already see the traffic?
text:
Where does OPDI already see the traffic?
To find the gaps, we ask a simple question of every European airport: of the traffic an airport is known to have handled, how much does Open Performance Data Initiative (OPDI) actually observe?
The two sources. The reference is EUROCONTROL’s published airport traffic statistics for 2025 — one row per airport per day, giving the number of departures (FLT_DEP_1) and arrivals (FLT_ARR_1) recorded that day. Against it we place the OPDI flight list of release v0.0.2, twelve monthly Parquet files in which each row is one flight reconstructed from crowd-sourced Automatic Dependent Surveillance–Broadcast (ADS-B) trajectories, carrying a departure aerodrome (adep) and an arrival aerodrome (ades).
How they are compared. The common unit is the movement: one departure or one arrival. A single flight is therefore counted twice — once at the airport it left, once at the airport it reached — which is exactly how the reference totals FLT_DEP_1 and FLT_ARR_1. Summing the OPDI flight list the same way, over the whole of 2025, gives a directly comparable count per airport.
What is calculated. For each airport,
\[\text{capture rate} = \frac{\text{movements OPDI attributes to the airport}}{\text{movements the airport reported}} \times 100\%\]
A flight whose trajectory begins or ends outside ADS-B coverage has no adep or no ades, and so contributes no movement anywhere. In 2025 that applies to 47% of departures and 44% of arrivals in the flight list, which is why a capture rate of 100% is not attainable in principle — the metric measures how much of an airport’s traffic OPDI can attribute to that airport, not the completeness of the trajectory data behind it.






The capture rate measures the detection algorithm as much as the coverage.
adep and ades are not reported by the aircraft; they are inferred from the trajectory. The algorithm of release v0.0.2, which built the 2025 flight list used here, lays an H3 grid of 30 NM radius around every aerodrome, keeps the state vectors below 4,000 ft, and assigns the airport whose reference point is closest to the start or end of the track. Full details are in the Release v0.0.2 section of Releases. Release v2.0.0 uses a newer method, which can also leave an airport undecided: see Departure and destination airports.
Two consequences follow directly, and both move the capture rate:

Aerodromes close together can be confused. Where several grids overlap, the nearest reference point wins and the runners-up are recorded as adep_p / ades_p. Paris Charles-de-Gaulle and Le Bourget, or Frankfurt and Egelsbach, sit well inside one another’s 30 NM grids, so a flight may be attributed to the wrong neighbour — inflating one airport’s capture rate at the other’s expense.
The algorithm is an iterative approximation. Successive versions have changed both the detection radius and the altitude ceiling, and a future refinement will attribute more flights at some airports and fewer at others.

A low capture rate is therefore a prompt to investigate — it may indicate absent ADS-B coverage, or it may indicate that the detection algorithm is mis-assigning that airport’s traffic.



Two summaries answer different questions. Capture rate is movement-weighted — of all the traffic in a size band, how much did OPDI see? Median airport weights every airport equally — what does the typical airport in the band look like? They diverge where a few outliers dominate.

The 40 NM figures above measure a single day. Tracking the same airports over time shows the effect of a deployment directly.
The chart below plots the daily capture rate at every airport hosting OPDI sensors: the share of an airport’s reported movements — one departure or one arrival — that the OPDI flight list attributes to it, measured against EUROCONTROL’s published traffic statistics. A rate near 100% means OPDI sees essentially all of the airport’s traffic. The full method, and the caveats that come with it, are set out under Where Next.

The red band marks a 5-day outage at Tbilisi, from 18 January to 22 January, with reporting resuming on 25 January. Only that airport goes quiet — its neighbours continue reporting throughout — so the cause is local to the receiver, not the data pipeline.

title: OPDI Sensors
text:
Overview
The OPDI Sensors is an initiative to extend the OpenSky Network crowd-sourced receiver network by deploying ground-based ADS-B sensors at strategic airport locations. The aim is to improve ground-based and low-altitude ADS-B coverage around airports, especially where existing coverage in the OpenSky Network is limited.
In collaboration with the Performance Review Commission, each deployed sensor receives ADS-B transponder signals from aircraft in its vicinity, providing position, altitude, speed, and identification data. The collected data feeds into the OpenSky Network and is subsequently used by the OPDI, enabling performance monitoring at airports that were previously unobservable through open data sources.
This page describes the network as it stands: where the receivers are, whether they are reporting, and how far each one sees. Two companion pages take the argument further — Impact on Airport Monitoring measures what the sensors added, and Where Next identifies the airports that remain unobserved.

title: Open Performance Data Initiative
text:
Much of the data behind aviation performance analysis is difficult to obtain, which makes results hard to reproduce and to build on. The Open Performance Data Initiative (OPDI), an initiative of the Performance Review Commission (PRC) in collaboration with the OpenSky Network (OSN), takes a different route: it builds a picture of air traffic from crowd-sourced Automatic Dependent Surveillance–Broadcast (ADS-B) signals, and publishes the data, the methods and the tools openly and free to use.
It works on three fronts:
The initiative is the work of a community of individuals — researchers, engineers and analysts — from institutions, universities, air navigation service providers and the wider open-data world. Everything they build — papers, datasets, source code — is published openly as resources anyone can use.

title: Point merge
text: A point merge system is an arrival procedure in which aircraft fly along an arc, called a sequencing leg, at a nearly constant distance from a merge point until they are sent directly to it; OPDI publishes the entry and exit of each leg and the passage of the merge point.

title: Point merge
text: A point merge system is an arrival procedure in which aircraft fly along an arc, called a sequencing leg, at a nearly constant distance from a merge point until they are sent directly to it; OPDI publishes the entry and exit of each leg and the passage of the merge point.

title: Point merge
text:
What it needs

A table of point merge systems kept with the pipeline: one row per merge point, with its coordinates, the distance band and levels of its legs and the dates it has been in use (136 merge points at 61 airports).
An arrival at one of these airports (the destination of the flight list), with positions within 60 NM of a merge point.

title: Point merge
text:
How it is computed

Candidates. Keep the reports within 60 NM of one of the airport’s merge points and at or below 25,000 ft; compute the distance and the bearing to the merge point.
On a leg. A report is on a leg when, over a 90 s window centred on it:

the distance to the merge point varies by at most 1.5 NM;
the mean distance lies within the listed band of leg distances, give or take 2 NM;
the bearing from the merge point turns by at least 8° (the aircraft moves around the merge point);
at least 80% of the reports have a ground track 60° to 120° off the bearing to the merge point (moving along the arc, not towards it).

Leg. Consecutive reports on a leg form a run. Two runs of one merge point at most 120 s apart, turning the same way about it, are one leg. The exit is moved forward report by report while the aircraft still moves along the arc and stays within 0.5 NM of the distance of the last accepted report.
Keep the leg when it lasts at least 90 s, ends at least 6 NM from the merge point, and the aircraft then comes within 3 NM of the merge point within 600 s. A leg shorter than 180 s must turn with the arc (a heading change of at least 30% of its bearing sweep), and no leg may climb more than 500 ft from entry to exit.
Direct. info.direct_aligned records whether the aircraft then flew straight to the merge point (ground track within 5° of the bearing for at least 60 s); it does not decide whether the leg is kept.
Merge point. pms-merge-point is placed at the closest approach to a merge point within 3 NM, once per approach, only when no take-off of the track lies between the passage and the landing that follows it (when no landing follows, when no take-off follows the passage), descending or level (at most 500 ft/min of climb), at 150 kt or more, and, where the system’s name and the landing say which, for a system that serves the runway landed on (within 30°).

Nothing is computed across a reception gap kept inside a track.

title: Point merge
text:
Based on

Developed for OPDI. A point merge system is a merge point with sequencing legs at a constant distance from it, which aircraft leave on a “direct-to” the merge point (EUROCONTROL); the rule looks for exactly that.
Comparable to the point merge detection of the traffic library (PointMerge), which also looks for more than 90 s at a nearly constant distance from a known merge point followed by a flight towards it. OPDI also requires the aircraft to move along the arc, within the published band of leg distances, and adds the checks of step 4.
The merge points and leg dimensions come from published navigation data and the EUROCONTROL Point Merge catalogue (each row of the table names its source).

title: Counting movements

title: Counting movements
text: The movement columns say which rows of the flight list count as a departure or an arrival, so that a flight cut into several tracks is counted once.

title: Counting movements
text:
What it needs

The departure and destination airports of each row, and the aircraft address.
The take-off and landing times, distance-circle crossings and highest altitude of the track’s events.

title: Counting movements
text:
How it is computed
A departure is often cut into two tracks: a short piece on the ground at the stand, then the flight itself. Both start at the airport.

superseded_dep is true when the row names a departure airport, has no take-off time, did not fly more than 1,000 ft above that airport, and the same aircraft departs again from the same airport within 3 hours (10,800 s). superseded_arr is the mirror for arrivals: no landing time, and the same aircraft arrived at the same airport within the 3 hours before.
movement_dep is true when the row names a departure airport, is not superseded, and there is evidence that the aircraft flew: a take-off time, a destination airport, a crossing of a distance circle, a climb of more than 1,000 ft above the airport, or a last position more than 40 NM from it. movement_arr is the mirror for arrivals.
No row is removed: the columns let users count, and choose.

title: Departure and destination airports
text: adep is the airport the flight left from and ades the airport it flew to, as four-letter ICAO codes, worked out from the trajectory alone, without flight plan or schedule.

title: Departure and destination airports
text: adep is the airport the flight left from and ades the airport it flew to, as four-letter ICAO codes, worked out from the trajectory alone, without flight plan or schedule.

title: Departure and destination airports
text:
What it needs

The cleaned reports of the track (see Cleaning of position reports): the first reports for the departure, the reports near airports below 6,000 ft for the destination.
Candidate airports: the large and medium airports of OurAirports, an open list of the world’s airports with position, elevation and whether they have scheduled passenger service. Small airfields and heliports are not candidates; records named as duplicates of another airport are left out.
For the correction (last part below): the runway events of the track.

title: Departure and destination airports
text:
How it is computed
Departures and arrivals use two methods, because the evidence differs. A departing aircraft is usually first received on or near the runway; an arriving aircraft is often lost by the receivers before it lands.

Ranking candidates

Candidates near a report are found with a grid of H3 cells of resolution 7 (each about 5 km²); the distance to each is then measured along the great circle.
An airport without scheduled service gets 10 NM added to its distance, so that a military or private field wins only when it is clearly nearest. The addition is not made when the aircraft is at that airport (flagged on the ground, or within 2 NM of it and at most 1,500 ft above it), unless an airport with scheduled service also lies within 2 NM.



Departure airport: the first report

Take the track’s first report and the nearest candidate (ranked as above).
Name it when the report is at most 30 NM from it and the aircraft is on the ground or at most 15,000 ft above the airport’s elevation.
A first report in the air (more than 1,000 ft above the airport and not flagged on the ground) names no airport when the track descends in its first 180 s (the altitude changes by less than −200 ft): it is an arrival first received on its descent.
adep_p lists the other candidates within 30 NM of the first report, in the order of the ranking.



Destination airport: the altitude trend

Take every report within 30 NM of a candidate and at most 6,000 ft above its elevation.
Smooth the barometric altitude over 5 consecutive reports (about 25 s).
Each report votes: climbing if the smoothed altitude went up since the previous report, descending if it went down. When descending votes outnumber climbing ones, the flight landed at that airport.
Of the airports it landed at, only those whose last nearby report is within 600 s of the latest landing compete (a stop earlier in the track does not). Among them the nearest wins, ranked as above; when two are less than 2 NM apart, the one the aircraft’s course points at wins.
ades_p lists other candidate airports near the end of the track, nearest first.



Correction from the runway events

After the events are computed, a runway event can replace an airport. The airport of a departure runway event (ATOT, line-up or take-off-roll) replaces adep only if it is the first departure event of the track and lies within 30 NM of the track’s first report with a position. The airport of an arrival runway event (ALDT or runway-vacated) replaces ades only if it is the last arrival event, comes after every departure event, and lies within 30 NM of the last report with a position. A runway-window time (info.method = legacy) never replaces an airport.
The source columns say how each airport was decided: aerodrome (from the trajectory), runway_event (from step 12), out_of_area or undetermined (no airport, as for an overflight).

OOA (out of area) is written only in data built for the European area: it means the track began (or ended) within 30 NM of the edge of that area, so the flight came from (or went to) outside it. With the default worldwide coverage the area has no edge, and such a flight has no airport.

title: First seen and last seen
text:
What it needs
The cleaned reports of the track (see Cleaning of position reports).

title: First seen and last seen
text:
How it is computed

Take the reports of the track with a measured position: one that the cleaning did not empty. OpenSky keeps sending an aircraft’s last state for about 300 s after it was last heard; cleaning empties these repeated values, so the last measured position is the last time the aircraft was heard.
first_seen is the first of these reports and last_seen the last.
A track with no measured position at all uses its first and last report with another measured value: a barometric altitude between −2,000 ft and 60,000 ft (the range the events use), a speed, a heading or a vertical rate. The GPS altitude does not count. A track with none of these uses its first and last report.
Each event takes the position, altitude and measurements of its report.
track_duration_min is last_seen minus first_seen, in minutes.

The flight list and the events read the same values in the same way, so the first_seen and last_seen of a track are identical in both. Every track has one first_seen and one last_seen event.
