title: Algorithms
text:
The Open Performance Data Initiative (OPDI) publishes, for each day, a flight list (one row per flight) and a flight events file (one row per event, a moment of a flight such as the take-off, with measurements such as the distance flown so far). Both are computed from the position reports of aircraft received by the OpenSky Network.
This section explains how each item is computed. There is one page per item, or per pair of items that are two ends of one thing (a start and an end). Every page has the same eight sections:
Processing steps shows the whole chain from the OpenSky archive to the published files. Units follow aviation use: altitudes in feet (ft), distances in nautical miles (NM, 1 NM = 1,852 m), speeds in knots (kt), vertical rates in feet per minute, times in UTC. Every column and info field is listed in the Data dictionary.
Availability and accuracy are kept apart. Availability says how often an item exists; accuracy says how close it is to an independent record when it exists. The column “Compared with” below says which records each item is compared with, where any exist, and the labels at a glance give, for every item, how often it exists and how close it is to the records.

title: Distance circle crossings
text: An xing-{radius}nm event marks each moment a flight crosses a circle of fixed radius (40, 50, 60, 100, 110 or 120 NM) around its own departure or destination airport.

title: Distance circle crossings
text: An xing-{radius}nm event marks each moment a flight crosses a circle of fixed radius (40, 50, 60, 100, 110 or 120 NM) around its own departure or destination airport.

title: Distance circle crossings
text:
What it needs

The departure and destination airports of the flight list, after the correction by runway events (see Departure and destination airports), and their positions from OurAirports. Circles are drawn only around these two airports.
The cleaned positions of the track’s reports.

title: Distance circle crossings
text:
How it is computed

For each report with a position, compute the great-circle distance to the departure airport and to the destination airport.
Dead band. A track running along a circle would cross it many times. A band of 1 NM on each side is used: the aircraft counts as outside the 40 NM circle only once it is more than 41 NM away, and inside only once it is less than 39 NM away. A crossing is the moment the side changes.
Interpolation. The time, position and measurements of the crossing are interpolated in a straight line between the two reports either side of the circle itself. Reports without a position are skipped. When the two reports are more than 30 minutes apart, no crossing is given. A report without an altitude takes its last known altitude, at most 30 s old.
Position jumps. A position that jumps away from the track and back (one or two reports whose steps to their neighbours imply more than 1,000 kt, with 2 NM of tolerance) is treated as missing. A crossing whose two reports still imply more than 1,000 kt is not given, unless no other circle lies between the two distances: the position then stepped and stayed (as near areas of GPS spoofing), and the crossing is kept with info.position_jump = true.
The bearing of the crossing point is computed from the airport.
Every crossing is kept and numbered in time order.

The flight list takes, for each radius, the first outbound crossing around the departure airport after the take-off (c40_dep to c120_dep) and the last inbound crossing around the destination airport before the landing (c40_arr to c120_arr). When the take-off or landing time is unknown, that time limit is not applied.

title: Distance circle crossings
text:
Based on

The circles are those of ICAO’s indicators (GANP KPI overview): KPI08, additional time in terminal airspace, measures from a 40 NM cylinder around the destination airport, with a 100 NM variant for airports where aircraft hold further out; KPI05, actual en-route extension, starts and ends en-route airspace at the same cylinders.
The crossing method (dead band, interpolation) was developed for OPDI and is the same as for the flight-level crossings.

title: Distance circle crossings
text:
What is published
Event types xing-40nm, xing-50nm, xing-60nm, xing-100nm, xing-110nm and xing-120nm (the family xing-{radius}nm), with position, altitude, distance_flown_nm and time_passed_s. Their info holds apt_icao, direction (inbound or outbound), crossing_seq, bearing, flight_level, bracket_s and, where it applies, position_jump (see the Data dictionary).
Flight list columns c40_arr, c50_arr, c60_arr, c100_arr, c110_arr, c120_arr, c40_dep, c50_dep, c60_dep, c100_dep, c110_dep and c120_dep (UTC).

title: Distance circle crossings
text:
Use cases

Additional time in the terminal area: aldt minus c40_arr (or c100_arr), compared with an unimpeded time per entry sector (info.bearing).
Where arrivals come from: the bearing of the inbound crossings around an airport, per hour.
Departure climb-out: the time from atot to c40_dep.

title: Distance circle crossings
text:
Limitations
The circles are drawn only around the two airports of the flight-list row, so on a track holding several flights the middle stop has none. See Limitations: distance circles.

title: Runway threshold crossing
text: xing-runway-threshold is the moment a landing aircraft passes over the runway threshold, the start of the part of the runway that may be used for landing, a few seconds before it touches down.

title: Runway threshold crossing
text: xing-runway-threshold is the moment a landing aircraft passes over the runway threshold, the start of the part of the runway that may be used for landing, a few seconds before it touches down.

title: Runway threshold crossing
text:
What it needs

An arrival runway pass (see Take-off and landing times).
Reports in the 60 s before the aircraft enters the runway area, because the report short of the threshold lies outside the runway itself.
The height above the ground, measured from the track’s own ground altitude (see Take-off and landing times).

title: Runway threshold crossing
text:
How it is computed

Take the reports of the arrival pass and those of the 60 s before it.
For each report, compute its distance along the runway centre line from the threshold of the landing direction: negative before the threshold, positive after it.
A crossing is the moment this distance changes sign, inbound. A dead band of 0.05 NM (about 300 ft) either side of the threshold confirms the crossing, so a report sitting on the line cannot trigger it twice. The time and position are interpolated in a straight line between the two reports either side of the threshold itself.
Keep one crossing per landing: the last inbound crossing of the pass, and only when the aircraft is at most 300 ft above the ground there. On a 3° approach an aircraft crosses the threshold about 50 ft above it. A low pass, an overflight or a circuit over the runway gives no event.

title: Runway threshold crossing
text:
Based on

Developed for OPDI, with the same crossing method as the flight-level and distance-circle crossings (a dead band, then interpolation).
The A-CDM Implementation Manual has no threshold milestone; its landing (milestone 6) is the touchdown. The code T16 in info.milestone is a label in the PRU flight diagram, not the manual’s number; see Milestones of a flight.
Thresholds from OurAirports.

title: Runway threshold crossing
text:
What is published
Event type xing-runway-threshold, with position, altitude, distance_flown_nm and time_passed_s. Its info holds apt_icao, runway, runway_bearing_deg, traversal_class (arrival), align_deg, max_gs_kt, milestone and height_reference (see the Data dictionary).
Do not confuse it with entry-threshold and exit-threshold, which are airport surface events of aircraft on the ground near the threshold markings.

title: Runway threshold crossing
text:
Use cases

Arrival flow over the threshold: count crossings per runway and quarter-hour for the landing rate actually achieved.
Spacing between arrivals: the time between the crossings of two consecutive arrivals on one runway.
Flare and touchdown: ALDT minus xing-runway-threshold of the same flight, when ALDT comes from the runway pass (info.method = acdm).

title: Runway threshold crossing
text:
Limitations
Missing when the aircraft was not received in the last minute before the runway or when its last report on approach was too high. See Limitations: runway events.

Availability and accuracy
No record gives the threshold crossing itself. It is compared with the recorded landing time, a few seconds later.

text: level-start and level-end mark the start and the end of each period in which the aircraft flies level, cruise included.

title: Level segments
text: level-start and level-end mark the start and the end of each period in which the aircraft flies level, cruise included.

title: Level segments
text:
What it needs

The cleaned barometric altitude, vertical rate and ground speed of the track’s reports (see Cleaning of position reports), with the same plausibility limits as the tops.
The elevation of the departure and destination airports, to tell flight from the ground.

title: Level segments
text:
How it is computed

Flight phases (level-start, level-end)

Phase of each report. Each report is given one of five phases by fuzzy logic: each phase has a rule that scores, between 0 and 1, how well the report fits it on three inputs, and keeps the lowest of the three scores. A rule is used only when all three inputs are known.

The phase with the highest score wins. The ground membership is measured from the lower of the heights above the departure and destination airports.
Smoothing. Each report takes the phase that is most common within 30 s before and after it (a 60 s window), which removes single misclassified reports.
Events. level-start is placed at a report in cruise or level flight whose previous report had another phase, and level-end at a report in cruise or level flight whose next report has another phase.
Checks. A segment shorter than 20 s (a single report, for instance) is not published. A report flagged on the ground, or less than 200 ft above the airport it is near, is never level flight, so there are no level segments on the ground or on the take-off or landing roll. The height is measured above the departure airport within 10 NM of it, and above the destination within 10 NM of the destination; for a report without a position, above the lower of the two airports. Farther than 10 NM from both, only the ground flag counts. So a level-off at 2,000 ft near a destination at sea level stays level flight, even after a departure from an airport 2,000 ft high.



Level segments of the vertical flight efficiency method
The tops and the level-offs use a second, geometric definition of level flight. These segments are not published as events of their own.

Interpolate the altitude in a straight line onto a grid of one point every 10 s, only between the first and the last measured altitude of each piece of the track.
A grid point is level when the altitude stays within a band of 50 ft over the next 10 s (a vertical speed of at most 300 ft/min). A point that lies between two measured altitudes more than 60 s apart is not level: the altitude there was not measured.
Consecutive level points form a segment, which ends 10 s after its last level point. Its altitude is its mean altitude. Segments shorter than 20 s are dropped.

Nothing is computed across a reception gap of more than 30 minutes kept inside a track: each piece is handled on its own.

title: Level segments
text:
Based on

Flight phases: the fuzzy-logic phase identification of Sun, Ellerbroek and Hoekstra (2017), with the rules and membership values of its code in OpenAP. OpenAP labels 60 s windows from the mean altitude, speed and vertical rate of each window; OPDI labels each report and then takes the most common phase within 60 s. The use of complete rules only, the ground height above the airports and the checks of step 4 were added for OPDI.
Geometric level segments: the rolling window of the vertical flight efficiency method of the EUROCONTROL Performance Review Unit (Peeters and Guastalla, 2017): a window of 10 s and 50 ft (300 ft/min) over altitudes interpolated in a straight line. The shortest segment, 20 s, is the minimum level time of ICAO’s KPI17 and KPI19 (GANP KPI overview).

title: Holding patterns
text: A holding pattern is a loop flown while the aircraft waits for permission to continue, usually before landing; OPDI publishes each one as a pair of events, holding-start and holding-end, with three measurements.

title: Holding patterns
text: A holding pattern is a loop flown while the aircraft waits for permission to continue, usually before landing; OPDI publishes each one as a pair of events, holding-start and holding-end, with three measurements.

title: Holding patterns
text:
What it needs

The cleaned positions, barometric altitude, heading and ground speed of the track’s reports, about one every 5 s.
The elevation of the destination airport, and the go-arounds, take-off and landing times of the same track. The departure and destination airports are those the flight list publishes, after its correction by the runway events (see Correction from the runway events): a flight whose destination the runway events change has its holds read as an arrival at the airport it landed at.

title: Holding patterns
text:
How it is computed
A hold turns through at least one nearly complete circle, always in the same direction, stays in a small area and keeps roughly one level. Turns given by controllers to space aircraft alternate left and right, a go-around climbs away, and a circuit flown by a light aircraft is low and slow.

Turn per report. For each report, take the change of heading since the last report with a heading, between −180° and +180°. A change across a silence of more than 60 s, or faster than 6° per second, is ignored. A report is turning at 0.4° per second or more.
Window test. Over a sliding window of 360 s (6 minutes), the window is flagged when all of these hold:

the turn, counted with its sign, adds up to at least 300° in one direction;
at least 80% of all turning is in that direction;
the first and last positions of the window are at most 8 NM apart;
the aircraft flew at least 15 NM in the window;
the altitude changed by at most 2,500 ft in total (the sum of all ups and downs).

The window is placed three ways (ending at the report, starting at it and centred on it), so an orbit shorter than the window is still seen whole. A window whose two ends are not 0.8 to 1.25 window lengths apart in time, because of a silence inside it, is not judged.
Height and speed. A flagged report counts only at least 2,500 ft above the airport and at least 140 kt over the ground.
Episodes. Flagged reports less than 120 s apart form one episode. It starts and ends at its first and last report turning in its main direction, so a lead-in turn the other way is not counted.
Keep or drop. An episode is kept when it lasts at least 240 s and its turn adds up to at least 330°. It is dropped when it starts or ends within 180 s of a go-around of the same track: repeated approaches are not holds.
Pattern. The hold is an orbit when less than 15% of its reports are straight, otherwise a racetrack (two straight legs joined by two half circles).
Context. info.context is arrival when the flight lands at its destination at most 60 minutes after the hold, which ends at most 150 NM from that airport; en-route when it lands, but later or further away; and other for a local flight (departure equal to destination, or no destination), no landing after the hold, three or more holds on the track, or holds making up more than half of the time in the air. Aerial work, survey, firefighting and training flights that circle fall under other.
Altitude. The altitude of the two events comes from the first and last report of the hold that has one.

title: Holding patterns
text:
Based on

Developed for OPDI, as a rule rather than a trained model. It draws on published work on holding detection, among it the traffic library and the detector of Olive, Basora, Sun and Spinielli (2024), and on the definition of holding procedures.
The rule was checked against the hand-corrected holding labels of Olive, Basora, Sun and Spinielli (2024), made on the arrival trajectories of Olive, Basora and Sun (2022). Holding procedures are defined in ICAO Doc 8168, PANS-OPS (as referenced by the Irish AIP).

title: Holding patterns
text:
What is published
Event types holding-start (first report of the hold) and holding-end (last report), with position, altitude, distance_flown_nm and time_passed_s. Both carry in info: holding_seq, pattern, direction (R or L), circuits, duration_s, distance_nm, altitude_start_ft, altitude_end_ft, straight_pct and context (see the Data dictionary).

holding_circuits
Number of loops: the total turn divided by 360°, to one decimal.

Holding delay before landing per airport: the sum of holding_duration_s of the holds with info.context = arrival, per day.
Where aircraft hold: the positions and altitudes of holding-start, which show the holding stacks of an airport.
Extra fuel: holding_distance_nm per aircraft type, as an input to fuel estimates.

text:
Limitations
Circling for other reasons (aerial work, training) meets the definition: use info.context. Holds below 2,500 ft above the airport or flown slower than 140 kt are not found. See Limitations: holding.

title: Off-block and in-block times
text: AOBT (actual off-block time) is when the aircraft starts to move away from its stand, usually pushed back by a tug, and AIBT (actual in-block time) is when it stops at its stand after landing.

title: Off-block and in-block times
text: AOBT (actual off-block time) is when the aircraft starts to move away from its stand, usually pushed back by a tug, and AIBT (actual in-block time) is when it stops at its stand after landing.

title: Off-block and in-block times
text:
What it needs

Reports of the track on the ground at the airport, with positions; most of the taxi must be received.
A passage through a stand (a marked parking position for one aircraft) in the track: the entry-parking_position and exit-parking_position events of the airport surface events, from the stands drawn in OpenStreetMap.
The take-off and landing times of the track (ATOT, ALDT, see Take-off and landing times), which tell the departure part of the track from the arrival part, and line-up and runway-vacated where they exist.

title: Off-block and in-block times
text:
How it is computed
The two sides are computed in the same way, one before the take-off and the other after the landing.

Movement on the ground

Reports that may be on the ground. Only reports flagged on the ground, without altitude, or at most 2,000 ft above the airport of their leg are read, so the flight itself is never read as movement on the ground.
Ground speed. About 40% of reports on the airport surface carry no position and under 1% a reported ground speed. The reported speed is used where it exists. Elsewhere the speed is worked out from the distance between a report with a position and the previous report with a position, when they are at most 30 s apart, and smoothed over three reports.
Moving or standing. A report is moving above 2 kt and standing at or below it. A report whose speed is unknown keeps the state of the last report whose speed is known. A movement ends at a report that shows the aircraft standing, or after more than 300 s without any known speed.
A movement counts only when it lasts at least 30 s; shorter ones are noise in the speed.



Parts of the track

The take-off and landing times cut the track into ground parts. The off-block time is looked for in the part before a take-off, the in-block time in the part after a landing. A track that lands, stands and departs again gets both. A track that never leaves the ground (no take-off or landing time and less than 30 s of reports in flight), such as an airport vehicle or a towed aircraft, gets no block time.



Off-block (AOBT)

Find the stand stop: the last stand passage of the part before the take-off that lasts at least 600 s (a shorter passage after the push-back is often where the engines are started).
AOBT is the start of the first movement that starts at or after the entry into that stand and is still going on 30 s later. Without a stand stop, it is the start of the first movement of the part.
The movement must start from a standstill: the report where it starts is at most 30 kt fast (the flag “on the ground” counts only when no speed is known). When the track starts with the aircraft already faster than that, the moment it left the stand was not seen and no AOBT is given.



In-block (AIBT)

Find the stand stop: the first stand passage after the landing that lasts at least 600 s, or that lasts until the end of the track.
AIBT is the end of the movement before the longest stop that overlaps that passage (a stop between two movements, or between the last movement and the end of the track). Without a stand stop, it is the end of the last movement of the part. The movement must end in a standstill, as in step 8.



Checks and the stand named

No block time is given on the runway: an AOBT less than 60 s before its take-off or between line-up and that take-off, or an AIBT less than 60 s after its landing or between that landing and runway-vacated.
A block time needs a stand passage somewhere in the track. It names a stand (and its airport) only from a passage in the same ground part that lasts at least 30 s or ends within a minute of the block time: the stand of the stand stop, otherwise the passage with the longest stay. A stand drawn in OpenStreetMap without a name gives no name.
The plausibility checks then remove a block time placed while the aircraft flies (more than 1,500 ft above the airport, faster than 80 kt and no report on the ground within 60 s), an AOBT at or after the take-off of its own part, and an AIBT at or before its landing.

title: Off-block and in-block times
text:
Based on

Movement on the ground: derived in part from the start-of-movement rule of the traffic library (StartMoving): moving above 2 kt for at least 30 s, with the speed worked out from positions and smoothed over three reports. OPDI also uses the reported speed where there is one, and adds the parts of the track, the stand stop and the checks. traffic’s push-back and parking-position detection is not used.
Definitions: AOBT and AIBT are the off-block (milestone 15) and in-block (milestone 7) times of the A-CDM Implementation Manual; taxi-out time is ATOT minus AOBT and taxi-in time AIBT minus ALDT, as in ICAO’s indicators KPI02 and KPI13 (GANP KPI overview).
Related work: Schultz, Rosenow and Olive (2022) set off-block when the aircraft is more than 40 m from its first position on the stand, and in-block when within 40 m of its last one.
Data: stands from OpenStreetMap, as for the airport surface events.

title: Off-block and in-block times
text:
What is published
Event types AOBT and AIBT, with distance_flown_nm and time_passed_s (interpolated from the events around them); they have no position and no altitude. The info of AOBT holds stand_exit (time of the stand exit used), stand, apt_icao, and the take-off of its part (take_off, take_off_method); that of AIBT holds stand_entry, stand, apt_icao, landing and landing_method (see the Data dictionary).
The flight list repeats them as aobt, aibt, stnd_dep and stnd_arr (see Milestone columns of the flight list).

title: Off-block and in-block times
text:
Use cases

Taxi-out time: ATOT minus AOBT of the same flight, per airport and hour; combine with an unimpeded time to estimate additional taxi-out time.
Taxi-in time: AIBT minus ALDT.
Stand use: how long each stand is occupied between an AIBT and the next AOBT of the same aircraft (info.stand).

title: Off-block and in-block times
text:
Limitations
Often missing, because they need reception on the ground at the stand, and the off-block time is late when the aircraft is first received already moving. In-block times sit about a minute after airport records given to the whole minute. See Limitations: block times.

title: Cleaning of position reports
text: Cleaning finds the values of the position reports that cannot be trusted and empties them (the value becomes missing, the report is kept) before any column of the flight list or any event is computed.

title: Cleaning of position reports
text: Cleaning finds the values of the position reports that cannot be trusted and empties them (the value becomes missing, the report is kept) before any column of the flight list or any event is computed.

title: Cleaning of position reports
text:
What it needs
The tracks (see Tracks and flight identity): seven fields of each report are cleaned, namely latitude, longitude, barometric altitude (from air pressure), geometric altitude (from satellite navigation), ground speed, heading and vertical rate. The identity fields (address, call sign, time) are never changed.

title: Cleaning of position reports
text:
How it is computed
Six stages run on each track, in this order.

Duplicates. Of two reports of one track at the same time, the one received last is kept.
Impossible coordinates. A latitude outside −90° to 90° or a longitude outside −180° to 180° is emptied.
Repeated values. ADS-B sends position and speed in separate messages, and OpenSky repeats the last value until a new one arrives, so a value equal to the one before was often not measured again:

latitude and longitude are emptied when the position was not updated (each state vector records when its position was last updated; without that time, when neither changed);
the barometric altitude is emptied when neither the position was updated nor the altitude changed;
ground speed, heading and vertical rate are emptied together when none of the three changed.

The first report of a track is never a repeat.
Spikes. For each field, the rate of change between two consecutive values still present (first difference) and the change of that rate (second difference) are compared with a limit. A value is emptied when it takes part in at least two over-limit changes of the same kind: the middle of a spike takes part in the jump up and the jump down, while a real step change takes part in only one and is kept.

The event detectors then also leave aside a barometric altitude below −2,000 ft or above 60,000 ft.
Three things are deliberately not done, because the PRC Data Challenges found that they made results worse: filling gaps with invented positions, removing positions disturbed by satellite-navigation jamming, and correcting speeds with weather-model wind.

title: Cleaning of position reports
text:
Based on

Follows the trajectory cleaning of the winning solution of the 2024 PRC Data Challenge, by Alligier and Gianazza (ENAC, team likable_jelly): the order of the stages, the repeated-value tests, the spike limits of the barometric and geometric altitude, the rule that a value is emptied when it takes part in two over-limit changes, and the 20 s rule for isolated values. Their spike filter is in turn adapted from the derivative filter of the traffic library. OPDI empties values instead of removing reports, and adds the duplicates, the coordinate check and the silences.
The three things not done are negative results reported by the winning team of the 2025 challenge (resourceful-quiver, 2025): completing trajectories always gave worse results, leaving jammed or spoofed GPS positions untouched gave better ones, and removing wind data improved their error.

title: Cleaning of position reports
text:
What is published
Nothing directly: the cleaned reports are not published. Every flight-list column, event and measurement is computed from them.

title: Cleaning of position reports
text:
Use cases

Reading OPDI events: a missing altitude or position on an event often comes from a value emptied here; it is “no data”, not an estimate.
Reproducing OPDI from the OpenSky archive with the same cleaning.

title: Cleaning of position reports
text:
Limitations
A spoofed position that does not jump (a frozen position) passes the cleaning, and a value emptied here is not replaced. See Limitations: tracks.

title: Cleaning of position reports
text:
Availability and accuracy
Not measured as a published item: cleaning affects the availability and accuracy of every other item.

title: Flight-level crossings
text: An xing-fl{level} event marks each moment the aircraft climbs or descends through flight level 50, 70, 100 or 245.

title: Flight-level crossings
text: An xing-fl{level} event marks each moment the aircraft climbs or descends through flight level 50, 70, 100 or 245.

title: Flight-level crossings
text:
What it needs

The cleaned barometric altitude of the track’s reports, with the same plausibility limits as the tops. A flight level is the altitude in hundreds of feet on the standard pressure of 1013.25 hPa: flight level 100 (FL100) is 10,000 ft on the altimeter.
Positions near the crossing, for its position.

title: Flight-level crossings
text:
How it is computed

For each level, follow the altitude of the track in time order.
Dead band. To ignore small movements around a level, a band of 300 ft on each side is used: the aircraft counts as above FL100 only once it is above 10,300 ft, and as below only once it is below 9,700 ft; inside the band it keeps the side it was last on. A crossing is the moment the side changes. A flight that levels off at the level itself never leaves the band and has no crossing of it.
Time. The time is interpolated in a straight line between the two reports either side of the level itself; the event’s altitude is exactly the level. Reports without an altitude are skipped. When the two reports are more than 30 minutes apart, no crossing is given, because its time cannot be placed.
Position. One of the two reports often has no position. It then takes the position interpolated between the nearest reports with a position before and after it, each at most 30 s away; otherwise the position stays empty.
Position jumps. A position that jumps away from the track and back (one or two reports whose steps to their neighbours imply more than 1,000 kt, with 2 NM of tolerance) is treated as missing. A crossing whose two reports still imply more than 1,000 kt is not given.
Every crossing is kept and numbered in time order (info.crossing_seq).

title: Flight-level crossings
text:
Based on

Developed for OPDI. The same crossing method (a dead band, then interpolation) serves the distance circles and the runway threshold crossing.

title: Flight-level crossings
text:
What is published

Their info holds crossing_seq, direction (up or down) and bracket_s, the time between the two reports the crossing was placed between (see the Data dictionary).

Climb and descent times: from ATOT to the first xing-fl100 up, or from the last xing-fl100 down to ALDT.

Traffic in the upper airspace: counts of xing-fl245 crossings per region.

Limitations
A crossing between reports far apart in time is an estimate (see info.bracket_s). See Limitations: vertical profile.

title: About
text:
The Performance Review Commission (PRC) was established in 1998 by EUROCONTROL’s Permanent Commission.
It provides objective information and independent advice to EUROCONTROL’s governing bodies on European Air Traffic Management (ATM) performance, based on extensive research, data analysis and consultation with stakeholders. Its purpose is to ensure the effective management of the European air traffic management system through a strong, transparent and independent performance review, as stated in Article 1 of the PRC Terms of Reference and Rules of Procedure.
The PRC reports to the EUROCONTROL Permanent Commission through the Provisional Council and is supported by the Performance Review Unit (PRU) operating under the EUROCONTROL Agency with the appropriate level of independence.
For more information about the PRC, see here.

title: About
text:
Open Performance Data Initiative
In 2022, the PRC launched the Open Performance Data Initiative (OPDI) with a view to establish a data platform, to support higher levels of transparency and reproducibility of performance related monitoring and associated analyses. This initiative addresses the requirement to establish a level playing field for all stakeholders, ranging from the interested public, operational and strategic planners, to political decision-makers. Pursuing an open data-based approach will allow all interested parties to tap into a harmonised data environment to build their assessments, validate results published by other parties, and reproduce findings in support of the political and operational discussion about observed performance.
The upcoming challenges to our industry require that stakeholders can embrace and tap into a harmonised and consolidated data set to drive the discussion on higher performance levels, performance expectations in terms of targets, or realised performance benefits following the deployment of new capabilities.
For more information about the OPDI, see here.
The data that the OPDI publishes are described in Data: what is in the files, how to reach them and where they have limits. How each item is computed, and how accurate it is, is explained in Algorithms.

title: About
text:
PRC Data Challenges
The PRC Data Challenges are an annual competition organised by the PRC that invites data scientists, researchers, and aviation enthusiasts to solve real-world aviation performance questions using open data. Each edition defines a specific prediction or estimation task, provides curated datasets, and evaluates submissions on a public leaderboard.
By engaging a diverse community of participants, the PRC Data Challenges advance the state of the art in aviation analytics while demonstrating the practical value of open performance data. Past editions have asked participants to predict the take-off weight of flights (2024), the fuel burnt over intervals of a flight (2025) and the taxi-out time of departing flights (2026).
See the Data Challenges page for details on each edition, or visit the PRC Data Challenge programme page.

title: About
text:
OPDI Sensors
The OPDI Sensors is an initiative to extend the OpenSky Network crowd-sourced receiver network by deploying ground-based ADS-B sensors at strategic airport locations. The aim is to improve ground-based and low-altitude ADS-B coverage around airports, especially where existing coverage is limited. The data collected feeds directly into the OPDI, improving the quality and completeness of open flight performance data.
The programme has sensors at airports in several countries, feeding into the OpenSky Network, with plans to expand to additional locations. Airport operators and aviation stakeholders interested in hosting a sensor are invited to get in touch.
See the OPDI Sensors page for the full deployment overview and information on hosting a sensor.

title: About
section: Benefits of Open Access and Open Data for Performance Monitoring
text:
Benefits of Open Access and Open Data for Performance Monitoring
To understand the depth of the proposed OPDI it is vital to define the key terminology upfront.

Open Access: Open Access refers to the process of managing copyright and licensing terms and access to the data. This access mode is vital to overcome today’s limitation and remove barriers such as price (including subscriptions, licensing fees, user-pay-principles, or even view fees), and permission (e.g., licensing restrictions) to enable free access and use of the data.
Open Data: The term Open Data refers to data—typically managed and available online—which is free of cost and accessible. Open data can be freely used, reused, and distributed provided that the data source is attributed.
Open-Source Software: Open-Source Software is software whose source code can be openly accessed, inspected, modified, and enhanced by anyone.

The focus of the OPDI is on open data, in particular open access and open use of data for non-commercial purposes. It is understood that potential developments of novel algorithms and techniques can produce tools that are made available to the community as open-source software.
There exists a huge body of literature highlighting the impact of open data. Across the different sources the following impact areas emerge:






Transparency and accountability





A key tenet of the performance-based approach is independent and impartial monitoring to provide the evidence for achieved performance levels and to identify and share best practice for further performance enhancements in ATM.
Higher levels of transparency and accountability provide the foundation for a democratisation of air traffic management. Public and stakeholder access to data is also seen as a key ingredient to establish accountability. This also requires a culture change that is implicitly built into the performance-based approach. Observed levels of performance are publicly communicated and tracked. Associated performance measurement algorithms are published and the monitoring results are reproducible.









Innovation, participation, and joint development





Open data from both public and private sources are adding a new dimension to the data revolution. It also is a key ingredient to realise the promises of big data, or supporting data-analytical advances in artificial intelligence/machine-learning.
A clear driver for innovation is the opportunity to understand how systems work, where bottlenecks emerge or certain patterns manifest. At the same time, it is important to understand the parameters and conditions for good and best-in-class performance. Sharing and access to data therefore fosters to have another view on performance by observing new developments with different priorities/perspectives, or other organisational/institutional factors limiting the use and value creation from data, including its combination with additional data and resources.
The ability of public, interested researchers, policymakers/think tanks, or strategic planners to access the data and exploit it creates joint communities of interest. This may enhance the value of the data to drive joint developments ranging from data standardisation, including access and storage, but also to build on the data. The latter may range from methodological approaches, operational solutions and other tools.









Effectiveness





At the heart of the performance-based approach is the potential to achieve higher levels of performance and associated decision-making through data-driven decision-making. This may affect day-to-day decision-making, but also long-term decisions such as the need for adopting new operational concepts or deploying operational capabilities.
Open data goes beyond the classical—potentially limited—sharing of data in support of use-case analyses, projects or activities. It is a continual process which allows to champion and demonstrate observed performance levels. In that respect open performance data can also serve as a tool to improve communication and partnerships in terms of data sharing.









Engagement and Empowerment





The most direct impact of open data for engagement and empowerment is related to its transparency effects. Air transportation and air traffic management are at a crossroad. Future political goals and expected performance levels require higher levels of transparency and the existence of a data basis in support of verification and validation/reproduction of results. The transparency discussion will result from a higher pressure on the industry to demonstrate—for example—its contribution to climate change and greenhouse gas emissions. There is also a discussion on the success of air navigation system modernisation (i.e., transformation) in general. This requires demonstration of operational performance benefits derived from funding and modernisation activities.
The need to address the societal challenges and political goals will require a wider engagement of air navigation with the public and policy level, but also facilitate such an engagement with the industry and interested public. The PRC is confident that the practice of the past to provide a platform to validate and reproduce performance observations will facilitate higher levels of engagement and empowerment with and between stakeholders and public. Open data can be a key enabler to facilitate this engagement and ensure the appropriate level of independent transparency to drive and inform the public debate, political and strategic decision-making.



Open data and performance analytics are often viewed as separate practices, however, both are inextricable when it comes to the operations of modern governance. To ensure transparent and independent review, open data provides the underlying raw material for the analysis and monitoring of performance. In that respect, the PRC’s OPDI aims at increasing transparency, supporting higher levels of data access and information availability for decision-making, engaging and increasing accountability of involved stakeholders.
For more information about the potential benefits of the open access and open data for performance monitoring, see here.
For questions about any OPDI activity — data, challenges, or sensors — contact pru-support@eurocontrol.int.

title: Limitations
text: OPDI is built from the position reports that the OpenSky Network’s receivers pick up: where no receiver hears an aircraft, nothing can be computed, and most limits come from that. A found event can still be wrong; a missing one says nothing about what the aircraft did (found is not the same as correct).

title: Limitations
text:
General limits

ADS-B reception
Everything in OPDI comes from ADS-B (Automatic Dependent Surveillance–Broadcast): radio messages in which an aircraft broadcasts its position, altitude and speed. The OpenSky receivers, run by volunteers and institutions, are on the ground, unevenly spread, and hear aircraft in line of sight: a few hundred kilometres away at cruise altitude, only close by near the ground.

No receiver near, no data: often over oceans, deserts and other areas with few receivers, and on the ground at many airports.
Cruise events are found almost everywhere, runway events at fewer airports, stand events at fewer still. A missing block time, runway event or surface event mostly means the surface was not heard, not that nothing happened (airports where ground events are nearly absent).
Aircraft without ADS-B, or not broadcasting it, are not in the data.
ADS-C reports, sent by satellite mainly over the oceans, are not used in release v2.0.0, so the ocean gaps stay.
Counts from OPDI (flights per airport, movements per runway) are lower bounds, not totals. The share of an airport’s traffic OPDI sees varies by airport and by day (OPDI Sensors: where next measures it over European airports in 2025).



Flights are tracks
OPDI uses no flight plans. A flight is a track: the position reports of one aircraft that belong together (Track identity), from where reception starts to where it ends.

Departure and destination airports come from the track, empty when it begins or ends away from an airport (Departure and destination airports). Small airfields and heliports are not candidate airports: their flights have neither, and no runway events.
Planned route, planned times and airline schedule are unknown: delays against a schedule cannot be computed from OPDI alone.
A flight split into two tracks gives two rows in the flight list.
An aircraft that lands and departs again under the same call sign, heard all the time on the ground, stays one track holding two flights; each item’s section says what this does to it.
Placeholder addresses sent by some transponders (000000, 000001, ffffff) can merge several aircraft into one track, which is not flagged.



Day of a flight
A flight belongs to the day it was first seen, in UTC, with all its events in that day’s files (Data).

To count the events or landings that happened on a day, read its files and the day before’s, and filter on event_time.
A flight first seen just before midnight UTC belongs to the earlier day, even if it took off after midnight.



Reference data

Records only in Europe. The items are compared with the airport operator records and Network Manager flight records that EUROCONTROL holds, which cover the European area; many airport records are to the whole minute (what OPDI is compared with). Outside Europe only how often an item exists can be measured, not whether it is right, and several items have no reference anywhere.
Open sources. Airports and runways come from OurAirports, airport layouts and stand names from OpenStreetMap, aircraft registrations, types and operators from the OpenSky aircraft database. Their errors and gaps carry over: a runway missing from OurAirports gives no runway events; unmapped taxiways, aprons and stands give no surface events, block times or stands; a stand drawn without a name gives no stand name.



Position errors and vehicles

Spoofing. Near areas where satellite navigation is disturbed (GPS spoofing), positions can jump, or step by 5 to 20 NM and stay. Jumps implying more than 1,000 kt are left out of the crossings and the distance flown; a spoofed position that does not jump (a frozen position) still misleads the detectors.
Vehicles. Airport vehicles and some towed aircraft carry transponders. Tracks that never leave the ground and have no aircraft type, or a vehicle type, are marked info.ground_only on their surface events and get no block times; they remain in the flight list.
Plausibility checks remove only events the track clearly contradicts; a wrong but plausible event stays.

title: Limitations
text:
Tracks and flight identity

When it is missing

A flight that no receiver heard has no track.
A flight heard in pieces far apart can be split into several tracks: a silence over 30 minutes stays inside one track only when both sides look like the same flight en route.



When it can be wrong

Two flights in one track, or aircraft merged by a placeholder address (Flights are tracks).
A call sign broadcast wrongly for a long time can split a flight.



What not to conclude from it

The number of tracks is not the number of flights: count with the movement columns.
flt_id is the call sign broadcast most often, which may differ from the filed flight plan.

title: Limitations
text:
Departure and destination airports

When it is missing

adep is empty when the first report is more than 30 NM from any candidate airport or more than 15,000 ft above it (first heard in cruise), and when a track first heard in the air descends.
ades is empty when the track ends without descending near a candidate airport (reception lost in cruise or far out).
24.2 % of the flights had no adep and 35.7 % no ades.
At a few busy European airports OPDI names the airport as destination of only a small share of the recorded arrivals (where no take-off or landing time exists).



When it can be wrong

At airports close together the nearest airport can be the wrong one, though the direction of flight decides between airports less than 2 NM apart.
A track holding two flights names only its first and last airports.



What not to conclude from it

An empty airport is not always an overflight: it can be a flight to a small airfield, or one whose end was not received.
adep_source and ades_source say how sure the answer is; runway_event is the most reliable.

title: Limitations
text:
Aircraft details

When it is missing

When the address is not in the OpenSky aircraft database of October 2024: aircraft registered later, military aircraft and many light aircraft.
17.2 % of the flights the Network Manager records had no type in OPDI.



When it can be wrong

When an address moved to another aircraft after October 2024, or the database entry is wrong.



What not to conclude from it

icao_operator is the aircraft’s registered operator, not necessarily the airline that flew the flight (wet leases, code shares).

title: Limitations
text:
First seen and last seen

When it is missing

Never: every track has both, identical in the flight list and the events. A track without any measured position takes them from its measured altitude or speed.



When it can be wrong

They are exact as reception times. A track holding several flights has one pair.



What not to conclude from it

They are when the aircraft was first and last heard, not its off-block, in-block, take-off or landing times.

title: Limitations
text:
Milestone columns and movements

When it is missing

Empty when its event was not found (see the event’s section).
aobt, aibt and the stand columns are often empty, because they need reception at the stand.



When it can be wrong

As wrong as the event behind it.
On a track holding several flights, the distance-circle crossings, block times and stands at the middle stop are not on the row; the runway events there are still published as events.
A row with no departure (or destination) airport can still have aobt and stnd_dep (or aibt and stnd_arr) from a block time at a named stand, with no airport to check them against.



What not to conclude from it

The movement columns (superseded_*, movement_*) have not been checked against official counts; two real short flights of one aircraft within 3 hours at one airport can be counted as one.

title: Limitations
text:
Take-off and landing times

When it is missing
When the aircraft was not received near the runway (airports far from any receiver have few times). Runway-pass times need reports on the runway or less than 1 NM short of it; runway-window times, within 5 NM and 1,500 ft of the airport.

A landing whose reception ends in the flare, before any report on the runway, can get no landing time.
A take-off first received more than 1,500 ft above the track’s ground altitude at the airport gets no take-off time.
Some busy European airports have no take-off or landing time at all on the three days measured, for a cause not established (where no take-off or landing time exists).



When it can be wrong

Runway-window times (info.method = legacy) are the first or last report of the climb or descent, so less precise: 94.3 % of the runway-pass take-off times and 91.5 % of the runway-window ones were within 60 s of the airport records; for landings, 97.1 % and 87.9 %.
Where reception starts at lift-off or ends over the threshold, the time comes from a report up to 1,500 ft above the ground; info.at_track_edge marks the track’s first or last report.
At a few airports the runway named, or the take-off time, mostly disagrees with the records (where an item is unreliable).
With no ground report at the airport, height is measured above the published elevation, so low or high pressure moves the 15 ft crossing (info.height_reference = elevation).



What not to conclude from it

The two methods have different errors: separate them with info.method when comparing airports.
A track keeps one ATOT and one ALDT per airport: on a track holding several flights, a second take-off or landing at the same airport is not published.

title: Limitations
text:
Other runway events

When it is missing

line-up, take-off-roll and runway-vacated need a report on the runway itself: where reception starts at lift-off or ends over the threshold, they are not published. line-up and take-off-roll are not given for a touch-and-go or a low approach.
xing-runway-threshold needs reports in the last minute before the runway, at most 300 ft above the ground there.
Runway crossings need ground reception on the runway.



When it can be wrong

When reception starts during the take-off roll or ends during the landing roll, line-up, take-off-roll and runway-vacated mark the first or last report received on the runway, which can be at high speed.
A go-around detector based on heights can count a training low approach, and misses go-arounds started above 1,500 ft.



What not to conclude from it

No reference gives line-up, take-off roll, runway vacated, go-around or runway crossing times: these events are not validated, only compared with the recorded take-off or landing.

title: Limitations
text:
Off-block and in-block times

When it is missing

Often: they need reception at the stand and on the taxiway, and a stand passage in the track. An arrival with no position or speed after the landing roll gets no in-block time.
35.0 % of the recorded off-blocks had an AOBT and 33.4 % of the recorded in-blocks an AIBT.



When it can be wrong

When the transponder is switched on during push-back, or the aircraft is first received already moving, the off-block time is the first movement received: late. A push slower than 2 kt, or a stand with few reports with a position, also makes it late.
Off-block times are often late: they differ from the airport records by a median of 99 s, and over the differences of up to 300 s are on average 78.6 s later. In-block times are closer: a median of 34 s, and on average 18.5 s earlier over the differences of up to 300 s.
Where a stand is drawn inside a larger stand area, the block times read the inner one.



What not to conclude from it

A missing block time does not mean the aircraft did not park.
Taxi times from AOBT are more often too short than too long, because a late AOBT is the common error.

title: Limitations
text:
Airport surface events

When it is missing

At airports without ground reception or without a mapped layout in OpenStreetMap. An area mapped without a name gives no info.osm_ref.



When it can be wrong

Vehicles: see Position errors and vehicles.
An entry at a track’s first report or an exit at its last is when reception started or stopped (info.at_track_start, info.at_track_end), not a movement.
Where a stand is drawn inside a larger stand area, both passages are published; the larger carries info.encloses_stand.



What not to conclude from it

A deicing_pad event means the pad area was passed, not that the aircraft was de-iced.
entry-threshold and exit-threshold are aircraft on the ground near the threshold markings (lining up), not the landing crossing of the threshold, which is xing-runway-threshold.

title: Limitations
text:
Vertical profile

When it is missing

Level-offs need both tops; tops need altitudes in the air.
A flight-level crossing needs reports with altitude either side of the level within 30 minutes. A flight that levels off at a crossed level has no crossing of it.
No level segment is published on reports flagged on the ground, or less than 200 ft above an airport within 10 NM of it.



When it can be wrong

A flight without a cruise (short, training) gets its highest report as tops; a track holding several flights gets one pair. A top at the edge of reception has info.observed = false.
The cruise of light aircraft splits into many level segments and level-offs, and the flight phases of slow aircraft are less reliable.
A crossing between reports far apart in time is an estimate: see info.bracket_s.



What not to conclude from it

None of these events is compared with a reference: no record gives tops, level segments or level crossings.

title: Limitations
text:
Distance circles

When it is missing

When the flight has no departure or destination airport, or reception does not cover the circle.
On a track holding several flights the middle stop has no circles.



When it can be wrong

A crossing across a spoofing step (Position errors) is kept when it passes one circle only, marked info.position_jump; larger steps give no crossing.
Circles are drawn on every leg of a track that holds several flights.



What not to conclude from it

Only the 40 and 100 NM circles are compared with airport records; the others are not validated.

title: Limitations
text:
FIR crossings

When it is missing

Where no position is received (oceans).
For stays shorter than 60 s in a region, which count as part of the region before.



When it can be wrong

The boundaries are those of one AIRAC cycle, 524 (28 November to 26 December 2024), for every day. An AIRAC cycle is the 28-day period in which changes to aeronautical data, such as airspace boundaries, take effect; crossings follow a boundary’s old line where it has moved since.
A crossing placed between two reports far apart in time (info.bracket_s) is an estimate.



What not to conclude from it

A crossing with info.vertical = true is a climb or descent between a lower and an upper region, not a lateral boundary crossing.

title: Limitations
text:
Holding

When it is missing

Holds below 2,500 ft above the airport, slower than 140 kt or shorter than 240 s are not found, nor holds cut by a reception gap.



When it can be wrong

Aerial work, survey, firefighting and training flights that circle meet the definition; they usually get info.context = other.



What not to conclude from it

Not every hold is arrival delay: use info.context = arrival for delay statistics.

title: Limitations
text:
Point merge

When it is missing

Only arrivals at the airports in the reference table are examined.
A leg cut by a reception gap, or shorter than 90 s, is missed.



When it can be wrong

At airports with several systems close together, a leg can be given to the wrong merge point.
pms-merge-point is linked to the runway landed on only where the system’s name says which runway it serves.



What not to conclude from it

pms-merge-point with info.via_leg false is an arrival that passed the merge point without a leg being found, not necessarily one sent direct.

title: Limitations
text:
Measurements

When it is missing

distance_flown_nm is empty before the first known position, and on tracks without any position.
time_passed_s is empty on an event earlier than first_seen.



When it can be wrong

Across a reception gap the distance adds the straight line, so it is a lower bound. Position jumps that imply more than 1,000 kt are not added (Position errors).



What not to conclude from it

Both count from the start of the track, not from the off-block or the take-off: a track first received in the air starts later. Use differences between two events of the same flight.

title: Data dictionary
text:
Release v2.0.0 is the upcoming release: its files are being produced, starting with the days from 1 January 2025. The data available today are those of release v0.0.2, described on Release v0.0.2.
Every column, event type and info field of the OPDI files of release v2.0.0 (default settings of the OPDI software), with the version columns and joins. For what is published, see the overview. The column tables come from the software’s own list of published columns, so they always match the files.

title: Data dictionary
text:
How to read the tables

Type: string (text), double (decimal), boolean (true or false), date or timestamp (date and time).
Unit: every time is in UTC (Coordinated Universal Time). Altitudes are in feet (ft), distances in nautical miles (NM, 1 NM = 1,852 m), durations in seconds (s) or minutes (min), angles in degrees.
An empty value (NULL) means the item was not detected or is not known. It never stands for zero.

title: Data dictionary
text:
Flight list
One row per flight. The file of a day holds the flights first seen on that day (UTC). A flight here is a track: the position reports of one aircraft that OPDI treats as one flight (see Tracks and flight identity).










Column
Type
Unit
Description




flight_id
string

Unique identifier of the flight. A flight is one track: the sequence of position reports of one aircraft that belong together.


icao24
string

ICAO 24-bit address of the aircraft’s transponder, written as six hexadecimal characters. It normally stays with one aircraft.


flt_id
string

Call sign broadcast by the aircraft, for example DLH123.


dof
date
UTC
Date of the flight: the day on which it was first seen. A day’s files hold the flights of that date.


adep
string

Departure airport, as its four-letter ICAO code. ‘OOA’ (out of area) when the track began at the edge of the covered area, so the flight departed from somewhere outside it. This occurs only in data built with European coverage. NULL when no departure airport could be identified, which includes every overflight.


ades
string

Destination airport, as its four-letter ICAO code. ‘OOA’ (out of area) when the track ended at the edge of the covered area, so the flight continued to somewhere outside it. This occurs only in data built with European coverage. NULL when no destination airport could be identified, which includes every overflight.


adep_p
string

Other airports near the start of the track that the flight could have left from, as a comma-separated list of ICAO codes, nearest first.


ades_p
string

Other airports near the end of the track that the flight could have gone to, as a comma-separated list of ICAO codes, nearest first.


adep_source
string

How the departure airport was decided. ‘aerodrome’: adep names the airport near which the track began, found from the position and height of its first reports. ‘runway_event’: adep was taken from a take-off detected on one of that airport’s runways, which takes precedence over the first method. ‘out_of_area’: adep is ‘OOA’. ‘undetermined’: no airport could be identified and adep is NULL, as for an overflight.


ades_source
string

How the destination airport was decided, with the same four values as adep_source: ‘aerodrome’ (found from the last reports of the track), ‘runway_event’ (taken from a landing detected on one of the airport’s runways), ‘out_of_area’ (ades is ‘OOA’) and ‘undetermined’ (ades is NULL).

string

Registration of the aircraft (its tail number), from the OpenSky aircraft database. NULL when the aircraft is not in that database.


model
string

Aircraft model, from the OpenSky aircraft database.


typecode
string

ICAO aircraft type designator, for example A320, from the OpenSky aircraft database.


icao_aircraft_class
string

ICAO aircraft description, for example L2J for a landplane with two jet engines, from the OpenSky aircraft database.


icao_operator
string

Three-letter ICAO code of the aircraft operator, from the OpenSky aircraft database.

last_seen

UTC
Time of the last position report of the flight received by the OpenSky Network.


atot

UTC

aldt
timestamp
UTC
Actual landing time: when the aircraft touched down at the destination airport. Taken from the flight’s latest ALDT event at that airport. NULL when no landing was detected.


aobt
timestamp
UTC
Actual off-block time: when the aircraft started to move away from its parking position. Taken from the flight’s earliest AOBT event. NULL when it was not detected, which is common because it needs reception on the ground.


aibt
timestamp
UTC
Actual in-block time: when the aircraft stopped at its parking position after landing. Taken from the flight’s latest AIBT event. NULL when it was not detected, which is common because it needs reception on the ground.


rwy_dep
string

Runway used for take-off, for example 25R. Taken from the same event as atot.


rwy_dep_bearing_deg
double
degrees
True bearing of the centre line of the take-off runway, in degrees clockwise from north. It describes the runway, not the heading of the aircraft.


rwy_arr
string

Runway used for landing, for example 07L. Taken from the same event as aldt.


rwy_arr_bearing_deg
double
degrees
True bearing of the centre line of the landing runway, in degrees clockwise from north. It describes the runway, not the heading of the aircraft.


stnd_dep
string

Parking position (stand) the flight left from, with the name it has in OpenStreetMap. NULL when it was not detected.


stnd_arr
string

Parking position (stand) the flight arrived at, with the name it has in OpenStreetMap. NULL when it was not detected.


c40_arr
timestamp
UTC
Time when the arriving flight last crossed, inbound, a circle of 40 nautical miles (NM) radius around the destination airport. NULL when no such crossing was detected.


c50_arr
timestamp
UTC
Time when the arriving flight last crossed, inbound, a circle of 50 nautical miles (NM) radius around the destination airport. NULL when no such crossing was detected.

Time when the departing flight first crossed, outbound, a circle of 40 nautical miles (NM) radius around the departure airport. NULL when no such crossing was detected.


c50_dep
timestamp
UTC
Time when the departing flight first crossed, outbound, a circle of 50 nautical miles (NM) radius around the departure airport. NULL when no such crossing was detected.

UTC

track_duration_min
double
min
Time between first_seen and last_seen, in minutes. Very short tracks are often pieces of a flight seen on the ground rather than whole flights. No row is removed on this value, so users can choose their own limit.


superseded_dep
boolean

True when this row is a piece of a departure that is already counted on another row: it has no take-off, and the same aircraft departs again from the same airport within 3 hours (10,800 s). False otherwise.


superseded_arr
boolean

True when this row is a piece of an arrival that is already counted on another row: it has no landing, and the same aircraft arrived at the same airport within the 3 hours (10,800 s) before. False otherwise.


movement_dep
boolean

True when this row counts as a departure: the row names an airport, it is not a fragment counted on another row, and there is evidence that the aircraft flew (a detected runway time, an airport at the other end, or a crossing of one of the distance circles). Use this column to count departures.


movement_arr
boolean

True when this row counts as an arrival: the row names an airport, it is not a fragment counted on another row, and there is evidence that the aircraft flew (a detected runway time, an airport at the other end, or a crossing of one of the distance circles). Use this column to count arrivals.


version
string

Version of the method that built this flight row, for example v5.0.0. It changes only when that method changes.


release
string

Name of the data release the row belongs to (v2.0.0). It is the same on every row of a release.




How the airports were found
adep_source and ades_source say how the departure and destination airport were found, with one of four values; Departure and destination airports explains each case.

aerodrome: An airport was named from the trajectory: from the first position (departure) or the descent near an airport (destination).
out_of_area: Departure only: the track began in the air near the edge of the area covered, so the flight came from outside it. Not used when the area covered is the whole world.
undetermined: No airport could be named.
runway_event: The airport was taken from a take-off or landing detected on a runway, replacing the value found from the trajectory.

title: Data dictionary
text:
Flight events
An event is a moment in a flight, with a time and a position. One row per event, in three parts:

the columns of the event, in the table below;
the measurement columns;
the columns of the event’s flight, as in the flight list (flight_id appears once, among the event columns; the flight’s version is flight_version, see Versions).











Column
Type
Unit
Description




event_id
string

Unique identifier of the event.


flight_id
string

Identifier of the flight the event belongs to. It matches flight_id in the flight list.


type
string

Event type, for example ATOT, level-start or xing-40nm. The data dictionary lists every type.


event_time
timestamp
UTC
Time at which the event happened.


longitude
double
degrees
Longitude of the aircraft at the event, in degrees (WGS 84, positive east).

double
degrees
Latitude of the aircraft at the event, in degrees (WGS 84, positive north).


altitude_ft
double
ft
Altitude of the aircraft at the event, in feet, from the barometric altitude the aircraft reports. For a flight-level crossing it is the flight level times 100. NULL for events that have no altitude.

string

Cell of the H3 hexagonal grid at resolution 5 that contains the event position. Cells cover about 250 km2 each, so the column can be used to select events in a region quickly.

string

Source of the position reports, OSN for the OpenSky Network.

string

Version of the method that produced this event type, for example events_v0.4.0. Different event types can have different versions.

Extra details about the event, as JSON text, for example the runway or the airport. The keys depend on the event type and are listed in the data dictionary.

Version of the method that built the flight’s row in the flight list (the version column of the flight list).

Name of the data release the row belongs to (v2.0.0). It is the same on every row of a release.



Every published event has a time. Events the aircraft’s own track clearly contradicts, such as an in-block time while it is still flying, are not published.

text:
Measurements
A measurement is a number attached to an event, stored as a column of the flight events file and empty where it does not apply (see Empty measurement columns).










Column
Type
Unit
Description

double
NM
Distance flown from the start of the track to this event, along the received positions, in nautical miles (NM, 1 NM = 1,852 m).

double

Time from the first position of the track to this event, in seconds.


holding_duration_s
double
s
Time spent in a holding pattern, in seconds. A holding pattern is a loop flown while the aircraft waits for permission to continue. It is set only on holding-end events and is NULL on every other event.

double
NM
Distance flown in the holding pattern, in nautical miles (NM). It is set only on holding-end events and is NULL on every other event.

Number of loops flown in the holding pattern: the total turn divided by 360 degrees, to one decimal. It is set only on holding-end events and is NULL on every other event.

double
NM
Distance from the aircraft to the merge point when it left the leg, in nautical miles (NM). It is set only on pms-leg-exit events and is NULL on every other event.

title: Data dictionary
text:
Event types
type names what an event is. A name with a part in braces stands for a family: xing-fl{level} covers xing-fl50, xing-fl70, xing-fl100 and xing-fl245. Each row links to the page on how the event is found and how accurate it is.

Take-off and landing

take-off-roll: The aircraft starts its take-off run. Line-up and take-off roll
ATOT: Actual take-off time: the wheels leave the runway. Take-off and landing times
xing-runway-threshold: The aircraft passes the runway threshold (the start of the landing part of the runway), a few seconds before touchdown. Runway threshold crossing
ALDT: Actual landing time: the wheels touch the runway. Take-off and landing times



Other runway events

line-up: A departing aircraft enters the runway to take off. Line-up and take-off roll
runway-vacated: An arriving aircraft leaves the runway after landing. Runway vacated
runway-crossing-entry: A taxiing aircraft enters a runway to cross it. Runway crossings
runway-crossing-vacated: The same aircraft leaves the runway on the other side. Runway crossings
go-around: An approaching aircraft gives up the landing and climbs away; placed at the lowest point of the approach. Go-around



Block times

AOBT: Actual off-block time: the aircraft starts to move away from its parking position (stand). Off-block and in-block times
AIBT: Actual in-block time: the aircraft stops at its stand after landing. Off-block and in-block times



Airport surface

entry-{element}: The aircraft enters an area of the airport. {element} is taxiway, apron, parking_position (a stand), threshold, hangar or deicing_pad, for example entry-taxiway. Airport surface events
exit-{element}: The aircraft leaves that area, for example exit-parking_position. Airport surface events



Vertical profile

top-of-climb: End of the climb to cruise, with the method of EUROCONTROL’s vertical flight efficiency indicators. Top of climb and top of descent
top-of-descent: Start of the final descent, same method. Top of climb and top of descent
level-start: Start of a period of level flight, cruise included. Level segments
level-end: End of that period. Level segments
level-off-climb-start: Start of a level-off during the climb: level flight below the cruise. Level-offs
level-off-climb-end: End of that level-off. Level-offs
level-off-descent-start: Start of a level-off during the descent. Level-offs
level-off-descent-end: End of that level-off. Level-offs
xing-fl{level}: A crossing of flight level 50, 70, 100 or 245, up or down. Flight-level crossings

A flight level is an altitude in hundreds of feet on the standard air pressure of 1013.25 hPa: level 100 is about 10,000 ft.


Distance rings

xing-{radius}nm: A crossing of a circle of 40, 50, 60, 100, 110 or 120 NM around the flight’s departure or destination airport (xing-40nm to xing-120nm). Distance circle crossings



Holding

holding-start: First turning sample of a holding pattern: a loop flown while waiting for permission to continue. Holding patterns
holding-end: Last turning sample of the pattern. Carries the holding measurements. Holding patterns



Point merge
A point merge system is an arrival procedure in which aircraft fly along an arc, called a leg, at a fixed distance from a merge point until they are sent directly to it.

pms-leg-entry: The aircraft starts flying along a leg. Point merge
pms-leg-exit: The aircraft leaves the leg towards the merge point. Carries the point merge measurements. Point merge
pms-merge-point: The aircraft passes closest to a merge point, within 3 NM of it. Point merge



Airspace

xing-fir: The flight passes from one flight information region (FIR) or upper information region (UIR) to another. FIR crossings



Track limits

first_seen: The first position report of the track. First seen and last seen
last_seen: The last position report of the track. First seen and last seen

Event types of release v0.0.2 that release v2.0.0 no longer publishes, such as take-off, first-xing-fl{level} and entry-runway, are listed with their replacements on Releases.

title: Data dictionary
text:
Fields of the info column
info holds extra details of an event as JSON text, for example {"apt_icao": "EGLL", "runway": "27R", ...}. The fields depend on the event type; a field without a value is left out. An empty info (an empty text) means the event type has no extra details.

Take-off, landing and other runway events
take-off-roll, ATOT, xing-runway-threshold, ALDT, line-up, runway-vacated, runway-crossing-entry, runway-crossing-vacated:

apt_icao: ICAO code of the airport.
runway: Runway direction used, for example 27R.
rwy_ident: The same, under the name used by earlier releases.
runway_bearing_deg: True bearing of the runway centre line, in degrees clockwise from true north.
traversal_class: Class of the runway pass: departure, arrival or crossing.
align_deg: Angle between the aircraft’s track and the runway, in degrees.
max_gs_kt: Highest ground speed during the runway pass, in knots (kt).
osn_flight_id: Call sign received during the runway pass.
milestone: Label of the moment in the PRU flight diagram (see milestones of a flight): T06 line-up, T07 take-off roll, T08 take-off, T16 threshold, T17 touchdown, T19 runway vacated. The PRU numbered them for this diagram only; they have no official status and differ from the A-CDM Implementation Manual’s milestone numbers. Not set on runway crossings.

height_reference: What the height above the ground was measured from: track (the aircraft’s own altitude on the ground at that airport) or elevation (the airport’s published elevation).
bracket_s: On ATOT and ALDT only: seconds between the two position reports the 15 ft crossing was placed between.

An ATOT or ALDT that could not be found on the runway is found from the climb or the descent instead (see Take-off and landing times). Its info holds apt_icao, runway and runway_bearing_deg (as above) and:

altitude_end_ft: Altitude at the end, in feet.

fir_to: The region entered.

bracket_s: Time between the last position report in the old region and the first in the new one, in seconds.

airac_validity_end: Last day of that cycle.

level-start, level-end, first_seen and last_seen have an empty info.

Identifiers and joins

flight_id (a flight, that is a track): The first 16 characters of the SHA-256 hash of the aircraft address, an underscore, and the time of the track’s first position in seconds since 1970-01-01 (Unix time), for example 3f9a0c1d2b4e5f60_1781412334.
event_id (an event): 32 hexadecimal characters, computed from the flight, the event type, the time and the version of the event. The same event gets the same identifier when a day is processed again.
icao24 (an aircraft’s transponder): Six hexadecimal characters, for example 4ca123.
flt_id (the call sign): As broadcast, for example DLH123.

Joins:

Flight events to flight list: on flight_id. Usually not needed: see Flight events.
Flight index to flight list: on flight_id; file names the daily flight list file that holds the flight.
Views of the release v0.0.2 shape: events.id is the event_id, measurements.event_id joins to events.id, and events.flight_id joins to flight_list_v0.id (the view and the Python reader both write it as id, in lower case).
OpenSky Network data: with icao24, the call sign and the time span from first_seen to last_seen, the position reports of a flight can be fetched from the OpenSky Network’s historical database, for example with the tools on its data tools page.

A flight_id depends on the method that built the track, so identifiers of different releases do not match: data of release v0.0.2 and v2.0.0 cannot be joined on flight_id. Join on icao24, call sign and time instead.
